By Adeel Hassan Ishani Desai and Isabella Kwai The global outage affecting Microsoft services reverberated around the world on Friday, upending services relied upon by millions of people. Parents struggled to contact their children’s schools, some government services faltered and many office workers could not access email as the disruptions stretched into a second day. Microsoft said in updates early Friday that it was making progress in fixing the problem. By 7 a.m. Eastern, it said that service was being restored to users in the Asia Pacific region, and was improving for users in Europe and North America. Still, major gaps persisted. A range of Microsoft tools were affected, including the email manager Microsoft Outlook, the workplace messaging and video calling app Microsoft Teams and the A.I. assistant Microsoft Copilot. By early Friday, Microsoft said that the core functions of Teams and Copilot were online. Corporate offices, government agencies and other services in dozens of countries were forced to adapt as workers struggled to complete the everyday tasks intertwined with Microsoft products. In Britain, the National Health Service said the outage was having a “disruptive impact” on its services. In Australia, intelligence and police forces said that their operations had been affected. Singapore told its taxpayers email capabilities had been disrupted, and the Supreme Court of the Philippines and the European Court of Human Rights said the outage could cause delays in their work. “It shows how reliant we are on these cloud systems,” said Dr. Timothy Wood, a professor of computer science at George Washington University. extraction.body: Massive Microsoft 365 outage disrupts Outlook, Teams, Copilot worldwide Apache HTTP Server patches critical HTTP/2 remote code execution flaw Microsoft is investigating a widespread outage affecting multiple Microsoft 365 services, including Outlook, Microsoft Teams, and Copilot, as users report connectivity problems worldwide. BleepingComputer has received numerous reports from users experiencing problems accessing Microsoft's services, including complaints that Outlook is down. According to Downdetector , which tracks user-submitted outage reports, complaints surged Thursday afternoon across numerous Microsoft services, including Outlook, Microsoft 365, Teams, Copilot, Azure, OneDrive, and the Microsoft Store. In a Microsoft 365 admin center advisory tracked as MO1550821, Microsoft confirmed that customers may be unable to connect to multiple services, including Exchange Online, Microsoft Teams, SharePoint Online, Microsoft 365 Copilot, and Microsoft Defender XDR. The company says the Microsoft 365 incident began Thursday at 1:26 PM ET, although it began investigating reports of Exchange Online mailbox connectivity problems in the Americas earlier in the day. Microsoft initially attributed the disruption to elevated infrastructure load across multiple regions, but has determined that the problem was caused by servers unexpectedly becoming unavailable. "We determined the elevated load isn't driven by an increase in traffic, but by a number of servers being unexpectedly unavailable; straining the remaining infrastructure. We're working to safely return them to service," Microsoft said in an update on X . The company says it has paused all deployments, redistributed connection traffic across its worldwide infrastructure, and is moving additional traffic away from affected systems to reduce load. While the company initially reported Exchange Online connectivity problems in the Americas, it later confirmed that users in any region could be affected. The outage follows a separate Microsoft Teams incident earlier Thursday that caused an outage for users in North and South America. That earlier incident, tracked as TM1550488, lasted from 9:45 AM to 10:53 AM ET and caused delays or failures when sending messages, errors creating or updating conversations, and problems retrieving chat messages. The company says the earlier Teams incident has been fully resolved. Microsoft has not indicated whether the two incidents are related, and the ongoing Microsoft 365 outage has not yet been resolved. BleepingComputer contacted Microsoft with questions about the outage and will update our story if we receive a response. Update 11/12/26 6:57 PM ET: Microsoft says it is seeing limited recovery from the widespread Microsoft 365 outage after successfully returning some affected servers to service. The company previously said its recovery efforts had not provided the expected relief and that it discovered a core process on affected servers was becoming overwhelmed, resulting in a loss of capacity. Microsoft also said it was investigating whether reverting a small number of recent configuration updates could accelerate recovery. "We're returning a portion of affected servers to the service, and they remain stable so far. We're also shifting traffic to alternate routes wherever possible and observing limited recovery," Microsoft said in its latest update on X . The company says it has streamlined the process of restoring the remaining affected servers and warned that users may experience a gradual recovery as their applications reconnect. Microsoft has not yet confirmed when services will be fully restored. Update 11/13/26 8:05 AM ET: Microsoft says its services are gradually recovering from the widespread Microsoft 365 outage, with improvements in email access and delivery. "We’re seeing encouraging recovery progress, with service availability and email delivery performance improving across a growing portion of affected Microsoft 365 infrastructure," Microsoft said in its latest update on X. "Some users may still experience intermittent issues as recovery actions continue." BleepingComputer has also heard from multiple Microsoft Exchange users who report that previously delayed emails have begun trickling into their inboxes as services slowly recover. Microsoft says it has extended its email timeout window to 48 hours to help preserve delayed messages while it works through email queues and backlogs. While service availability continues to improve, Microsoft warns that some users may still experience intermittent connectivity problems as recovery efforts continue across the remaining affected infrastructure. Yet when major outages happen, we're left wondering whether AI-generated code, poor testing, or underlying software issues played a role. With Microsoft, the explanation always seems to be "server overload" or "increased demand." Rarely do we hear a straightforward admission of deeper engineering problems. If AI is truly as capable as Microsoft claims, why not use it to fix longstanding bugs, optimise Windows, eliminate unnecessary bloat, and address the endless stream of security vulnerabilities? After decades of development, Microsoft's software is still bloated, resource-hungry, and riddled with security issues. The cycle never seems to end. **Perhaps Microsoft should focus less on replacing engineers with AI and more on using AI to build reliable, secure, and efficient software.** AI hype is easy. extraction.body: Around 10:40 am ET on Thursday, Microsoft posted on its 365 status page on X that it was “investigating reports of users experiencing issues when accessing or using Microsoft Teams functionality in North America.” By just before 1 pm ET, it said it was aware of “issues accessing Exchange Online mailboxes through multiple connection methods in the Americas.” Microsoft later said that its network was also “experiencing elevated load across multiple regions, which is likely contributing to the connectivity errors,” but that the issue was related to servers going offline, not due to increased traffic. Around an hour later, Microsoft said it had “begun redistributing connection traffic across our broader worldwide infrastructure to help balance the load” and was “aggressively pursuing all pathways to reduce impact.” “We've paused all deployments. We're moving additional traffic off the affected infrastructure, and we're restarting affected servers to return them to service,” Microsoft wrote. In an update on its status page, Microsoft said impacted services may include Exchange Online, Microsoft Teams, SharePoint Online, Microsoft Copilot 365, and Microsoft Defender XDR. “We are aware and investigating reports of users experiencing issues with Microsoft 365 services, primarily issues with Exchange Online,” a Microsoft spokesperson tells WIRED in a statement. “We appreciate our customer's patience while we work to restore services as soon as possible.” Outage reports on the service uptime tracking website Downdetector began falling around 1:15 pm ET after a large spike in users reporting issues with Outlook and other Microsoft 365 products around noon. It is currently unclear when the outage may be over or what its cause may be. In a status update on X posted just before 3 pm ET, Microsoft said “a problem” was “causing servers to fail automated health checks and become unavailable” but that it was attempting to reboot its systems to hopefully bring them back online. Configuration errors, resolution issues with the Domain Name System, and cyberattacks can all cause connection errors. There is currently no indication that a cyberattack caused the current Microsoft outage. While major Microsoft outages are relatively rare, they are far from unprecedented. In July 2024, a corrupted update from the security firm CrowdStrike caused the “blues screen of death” on Windows machines around the world, while a separate but nearly simultaneous outage knocked out Microsoft Azure services for hours, causing untold millions of dollars in lost revenue due to companies’ inability to function as normal. Updated 11/12/2026 at 3:05 pm ET: Added comment from Microsoft. Updated 11/12/2026 at 5:20 pm ET: WIRED updated the article to clarify that the Azure outage was unrelated to the CrowdStrike-related issues with Windows in 2024.

Parents struggled to contact their children’s schools, some government services faltered and many office workers could not access email as the disruptions stretched into a second day. Microsoft said in updates early Friday that it was making progress in fixing the problem. By 7 a.m. Eastern, it said that service was being restored to users in the Asia Pacific region, and was improving for users in Europe and North America. Still, major gaps persisted. A range of Microsoft tools were affected, including the email manager Microsoft Outlook, the workplace messaging and video calling app Microsoft Teams and the A.I. assistant Microsoft Copilot. By early Friday, Microsoft said that the core functions of Teams and Copilot were online. Corporate offices, government agencies and other services in dozens of countries were forced to adapt as workers struggled to complete the everyday tasks intertwined with Microsoft products. Singapore told its taxpayers email capabilities had been disrupted, and the Supreme Court of the Philippines and the European Court of Human Rights said the outage could cause delays in their work. “It shows how reliant we are on these cloud systems,” said Dr. Timothy Wood, a professor of computer science at George Washington University. According to Downdetector , which tracks user-submitted outage reports, complaints surged Thursday afternoon across numerous Microsoft services, including Outlook, Microsoft 365, Teams, Copilot, Azure, OneDrive, and the Microsoft Store. In a Microsoft 365 admin center advisory tracked as MO1550821, Microsoft confirmed that customers may be unable to connect to multiple services, including Exchange Online, Microsoft Teams, SharePoint Online, Microsoft 365 Copilot, and Microsoft Defender XDR. The company says the Microsoft 365 incident began Thursday at 1:26 PM ET, although it began investigating reports of Exchange Online mailbox connectivity problems in the Americas earlier in the day. Microsoft initially attributed the disruption to elevated infrastructure load across multiple regions, but has determined that the problem was caused by servers unexpectedly becoming unavailable. "We determined the elevated load isn't driven by an increase in traffic, but by a number of servers being unexpectedly unavailable; straining the remaining infrastructure. We're working to safely return them to service," Microsoft said in an update on X . The company says it has paused all deployments, redistributed connection traffic across its worldwide infrastructure, and is moving additional traffic away from affected systems to reduce load. While the company initially reported Exchange Online connectivity problems in the Americas, it later confirmed that users in any region could be affected. The outage follows a separate Microsoft Teams incident earlier Thursday that caused an outage for users in North and South America. That earlier incident, tracked as TM1550488, lasted from 9:45 AM to 10:53 AM ET and caused delays or failures when sending messages, errors creating or updating conversations, and problems retrieving chat messages. The company says the earlier Teams incident has been fully resolved. Microsoft has not indicated whether the two incidents are related, and the ongoing Microsoft 365 outage has not yet been resolved. BleepingComputer contacted Microsoft with questions about the outage and will update our story if we receive a response. Update 11/12/26 6:57 PM ET: Microsoft says it is seeing limited recovery from the widespread Microsoft 365 outage after successfully returning some affected servers to service. The company previously said its recovery efforts had not provided the expected relief and that it discovered a core process on affected servers was becoming overwhelmed, resulting in a loss of capacity. Microsoft also said it was investigating whether reverting a small number of recent configuration updates could accelerate recovery. "We're returning a portion of affected servers to the service, and they remain stable so far. We're also shifting traffic to alternate routes wherever possible and observing limited recovery," Microsoft said in its latest update on X . The company says it has streamlined the process of restoring the remaining affected servers and warned that users may experience a gradual recovery as their applications reconnect. Microsoft has not yet confirmed when services will be fully restored. Update 11/13/26 8:05 AM ET: Microsoft says its services are gradually recovering from the widespread Microsoft 365 outage, with improvements in email access and delivery. "We’re seeing encouraging recovery progress, with service availability and email delivery performance improving across a growing portion of affected Microsoft 365 infrastructure," Microsoft said in its latest update on X. "Some users may still experience intermittent issues as recovery actions continue." BleepingComputer has also heard from multiple Microsoft Exchange users who report that previously delayed emails have begun trickling into their inboxes as services slowly recover. Microsoft says it has extended its email timeout window to 48 hours to help preserve delayed messages while it works through email queues and backlogs. While service availability continues to improve, Microsoft warns that some users may still experience intermittent connectivity problems as recovery efforts continue across the remaining affected infrastructure. Microsoft has not yet responded to BleepingComputer's questions about the root cause of the outage and whether it is related to Thursday's earlier Teams disruption. Yet when major outages happen, we're left wondering whether AI-generated code, poor testing, or underlying software issues played a role. With Microsoft, the explanation always seems to be "server overload" or "increased demand." Rarely do we hear a straightforward admission of deeper engineering problems. If AI is truly as capable as Microsoft claims, why not use it to fix longstanding bugs, optimise Windows, eliminate unnecessary bloat, and address the endless stream of security vulnerabilities? After decades of development, Microsoft's software is still bloated, resource-hungry, and riddled with security issues. Every Patch Tuesday, Microsoft fixes a bunch of vulnerabilities, only for another batch to appear the following month. The cycle never seems to end. **Perhaps Microsoft should focus less on replacing engineers with AI and more on using AI to build reliable, secure, and efficient software.** AI hype is easy. Engineering quality is what actually matters.

passages: “We appreciate our customer's patience while we work to restore services as soon as possible.” Outage reports on the service uptime tracking website Downdetector began falling around 1:15 pm ET after a large spike in users reporting issues with Outlook and other Microsoft 365 products around noon.
While major Microsoft outages are relatively rare, they are far from unprecedented.

In July 2024, a corrupted update from the security firm CrowdStrike caused the “blues screen of death” on Windows machines around the world, while a separate but nearly simultaneous outage knocked out Microsoft Azure services for hours, causing untold millions of dollars in lost revenue due to companies’ inability to function as normal.
There is currently no indication that a cyberattack caused the current Microsoft outage.

extraction.body: Around 10:40 am ET on Thursday, Microsoft posted on its 365 status page on X that it was “investigating reports of users experiencing issues when accessing or using Microsoft Teams functionality in North America.” By just before 1 pm ET, it said it was aware of “issues accessing Exchange Online mailboxes through multiple connection methods in the Americas.” Microsoft later said that its network was also “experiencing elevated load across multiple regions, which is likely contributing to the connectivity errors,” but that the issue was related to servers going offline, not due to increased traffic. Around an hour later, Microsoft said it had “begun redistributing connection traffic across our broader worldwide infrastructure to help balance the load” and was “aggressively pursuing all pathways to reduce impact.” “We've paused all deployments. We're moving additional traffic off the affected infrastructure, and we're restarting affected servers to return them to service,” Microsoft wrote. In an update on its status page, Microsoft said impacted services may include Exchange Online, Microsoft Teams, SharePoint Online, Microsoft Copilot 365, and Microsoft Defender XDR. “We are aware and investigating reports of users experiencing issues with Microsoft 365 services, primarily issues with Exchange Online,” a Microsoft spokesperson tells WIRED in a statement. “We appreciate our customer's patience while we work to restore services as soon as possible.” Outage reports on the service uptime tracking website Downdetector began falling around 1:15 pm ET after a large spike in users reporting issues with Outlook and other Microsoft 365 products around noon. It is currently unclear when the outage may be over or what its cause may be. In a status update on X posted just before 3 pm ET, Microsoft said “a problem” was “causing servers to fail automated health checks and become unavailable” but that it was attempting to reboot its systems to hopefully bring them back online. Configuration errors, resolution issues with the Domain Name System, and cyberattacks can all cause connection errors. extraction.body: The abrupt resignation of Nvidia’s chief executive, Jensen Huang, on Thursday morning after revelations that he had extramarital affairs with two women sent shock waves through the A.I. industry and spurred calls on Capitol Hill for investigations into whether U.S. security had been compromised. Mr. Huang, the co-founder and chief executive of the Silicon Valley chip giant, stepped down after Nvidia’s board started an inquiry into allegations that he had extramarital affairs with a woman who U.S. intelligence agencies have concluded was spying for China, as well as with an executive who reported to him. It was the stunning fall of one of the most powerful figures in the A.I. boom. Nvidia controls an estimated 90 percent of the market for the advanced chips that are an essential component of artificial intelligence projects. It also touched the White House, where Mr. Huang long had a firm ally in President Trump. The president defended Mr. Huang all week and praised him again on Thursday for doing a “fantastic job”; Mr. Trump then recommended that Tim Cook, the former Apple chief executive, take the helm at Nvidia. A series of reports by The New York Times showed that Mr. Huang, 63, had a relationship with Alice Huang, a Chinese businesswoman who had been recruited by China’s main spy agency to gather information on Mr. Huang. The Times also reported that Mr. Trump had been warned about the relationship but took no action. U.S. officials suspect that Megaspeed, the Singaporean company where Ms. Huang was a top executive, has helped to smuggle restricted chips into China. Ms. Huang has not responded to requests for comment; China has rejected the espionage claims and called the smuggling allegations “smears.” On Capitol Hill, Democrats called for an investigation into whether Mr. Huang had compromised U.S. national security. Senator Chuck Schumer of New York, the minority leader, said the Trump administration also “must answer for what it did once it learned about Mr. Huang’s relationship with a suspected Chinese intelligence asset.” Senator John Thune, Republican of South Dakota and the majority leader, said on Thursday that he anticipated Mr. Huang’s resignation would not keep Congress from conducting hearings on his relationship with a suspected Chinese spy. “It would make sense because of the nature of the association,” he said. Nvidia’s board : The board did not mention Mr. Huang’s conduct in its statement announcing his resignation. Instead, it thanked him for his “immeasurable contributions to the company and the industry.” Colette Kress, Nvidia’s chief financial officer , will serve as interim chief executive while the search for a permanent replacement is carried out, it said. Another affair: Mr. Huang had a second extramarital relationship with an executive who reported to him, according to five people who worked at the company, The Times reported on Wednesday. He is the latest member to join a growing club of chief executives brought down by affairs. A long-term strategy: China’s intelligence services have for decades used romantic entanglements to compromise or extract information from prominent people. Although the use of seduction in espionage is not unique to China, the country’s use of it differs in the amount of time it is willing to invest. Read more › Mr. Huang resigned as Nvidia’s chief executive on Thursday. But that has not appeared to slow a bipartisan push for more information on whether he had compromised national security. Senator Chuck Schumer of New York, the Democratic leader, said in a social media post that Congress must “demand answers” from Mr. Huang. Mr. Schumer also called on the Trump administration to “answer for what it did once it learned about Mr. Huang’s relationship with a suspected Chinese intelligence asset.” Mr. Lutnick’s department was required to review companies for national security risks before the Trump administration allowed Nvidia to sell advanced chips to China last year. The top Democrats on two congressional committees also wrote to Mr. Lutnick on Thursday, saying they were investigating the matter. My colleagues and I went on Hard Fork, the New York Times podcast about the future of technology, to discuss Jensen Huang’s resignation and its impact on the global tech industry. Listen to or watch it here . House Republicans said they were in discussions with Jensen Huang to get him to testify before Congress sometime this month. Representatives Brian Mast of Florida, who leads the Foreign Affairs Committee, and John Mooelnar of Michigan, who leads a different House committee focused on China, separately told reporters that they had been working to confirm a date and format for Huang to discuss allegations that he had an affair with a woman who U.S. intelligence agencies have concluded was spying for China. Huang’s testimony is not yet scheduled, and it is not clear whether his testimony would be public. Nvidia shares recovered most of their losses in the market by the close of trading, finishing more than 4 percent lower. The stock had fallen by as much as 14 percent Thursday morning after the resignation of Jensen Huang was announced. But as investors’ fears about the company’s future without Huang eased, the shares rebounded. Jensen Huang’s resignation may take down another victim: the movement to build open source A.I. systems, according to a report from SemiAnalysis, a prominent A.I. research group. Huang has been a champion for developing A.I. systems with public underlying code that are cheaper to run. The most advanced open source systems have been developed in China, using Nvidia chips, SemiAnalysis said. The U.S. open source ecosystem, as well as many American start-ups, rely on those Chinese models. “This is significantly impaired with Jensen gone,” the analysts wrote. Mr. Huang, the co-founder and chief executive of the Silicon Valley chip giant, stepped down after Nvidia’s board started an inquiry into allegations that he had extramarital affairs with a woman who U.S. intelligence agencies have concluded was spying for China, as well as with an executive who reported to him.

It was the stunning fall of one of the most powerful figures in the A.I. boom. Nvidia controls an estimated 90 percent of the market for the advanced chips that are an essential component of artificial intelligence projects.

passages: “They’re just playing right in the hands of a lot of people that don’t want to see it happen,” Trump said. “That could be political people.

I didn’t even know how you felt about it.
Correction: TechCrunch mischaracterized Tan’s political leanings in an earlier version of this post.
Tan, a self-described San Francisco Democrat, had previously said he was hopeful about Trump and has a nuanced position on the current administration.

“I’m onstage with the besties,” Huang told Trump, referring to the venture capitalists who host the podcast All-In , including tech investors Chamath Palihapitiya, Jason Calacanis, and White House advisers David Friedberg and David Sacks .

Trump and others, like Y Combinator CEO Garry Tan, have stated their belief that the growing sentiment against data center construction is part of an international psyop to stifle American economic growth.

In a move that will spark night terrors for public relations professionals everywhere, Huang flaunted his comfort with the president by putting Trump on speaker for conference attendees to hear.

I didn’t even know how you felt about it. I just hoped you felt the same way as me. We’re going to lead.”

coreStoryFacts.text: Huang admits the affair, Nvidia’s board says it will conduct an investigation.
Huang also had a relationship with Kimberly Powell , Nvidia’s vice president of health care, who reports to him.

Over the past week, some of Silicon Valley’s most influential investors had argued that America could not win the A.I. race without Jensen Huang, casting his relationship with a woman believed to be a Chinese spy as a personal lapse that should be forgiven because of his importance to the industry.
“Sadly, greatness doesn’t guarantee goodness,” Sarah Guo, a venture capitalist, wrote on X late Wednesday.
On Thursday, she called his resignation “a big loss.”
October 2026: Mr. Huang’s affair with Ms. Huang is reported in The New York Times .
Trump had been warned about the relationship but took no action.

Senator John Thune, Republican of South Dakota and the majority leader, told reporters at the Capitol on Thursday that he anticipated Congress would conduct oversight into Jensen Huang’s apparent involvement with an alleged Chinese spy, even though Huang has resigned as chief executive of Nvidia.
Huang was resigning from the company he had led for 33 years.
The stock had fallen by as much as 14 percent Thursday morning after the resignation of Jensen Huang was announced.

The Democratic leader, Senator Chuck Schumer of New York, said in a social media post that Congress must “demand answers” from Huang and Nvidia officials about “how they may have put U.S. national security at risk.” He added the Trump administration “must answer for what it did once it learned about Mr.
House Republicans said they were in discussions with Jensen Huang to get him to testify before Congress sometime this month.

Representatives Brian Mast of Florida, who leads the Foreign Affairs Committee, and John Mooelnar of Michigan, who leads a different House committee focused on China, separately told reporters that they had been working to confirm a date and format for Huang to discuss allegations that he had an affair with a woman who U.S. intelligence agencies have concluded was spying for China.
Huang in charge, Nvidia’s role could change, Mr.
“They’re just playing right in the hands of a lot of people that don’t want to see it happen,” Trump said. “That could be political people.
And we’re not going to let that happen.
While Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang was onstage at the All-In Summit on Monday morning in Los Angeles, he got a phone call that he couldn’t send to voicemail — it was from President Donald Trump.
I didn’t even know how you felt about it.
Correction: TechCrunch mischaracterized Tan’s political leanings in an earlier version of this post.
Tan, a self-described San Francisco Democrat, had previously said he was hopeful about Trump and has a nuanced position on the current administration.

“I’m onstage with the besties,” Huang told Trump, referring to the venture capitalists who host the podcast All-In , including tech investors Chamath Palihapitiya, Jason Calacanis, and White House advisers David Friedberg and David Sacks .

Trump and others, like Y Combinator CEO Garry Tan, have stated their belief that the growing sentiment against data center construction is part of an international psyop to stifle American economic growth.
But the source of the public’s concern is more straightforward.

Recent Gallup polling shows that seven in 10 Americans oppose the construction of data centers in their area , with more than 50% of respondents citing the effect of data centers on environmental resources .

extraction.body: The abrupt resignation of Nvidia’s chief executive, Jensen Huang, on Thursday morning after revelations that he had extramarital affairs with two women sent shock waves through the A.I. industry and spurred calls on Capitol Hill for investigations into whether U.S. security had been compromised. Mr. Huang, the co-founder and chief executive of the Silicon Valley chip giant, stepped down after Nvidia’s board started an inquiry into allegations that he had extramarital affairs with a woman who U.S. intelligence agencies have concluded was spying for China, as well as with an executive who reported to him. It was the stunning fall of one of the most powerful figures in the A.I. boom. Nvidia controls an estimated 90 percent of the market for the advanced chips that are an essential component of artificial intelligence projects. It also touched the White House, where Mr. Huang long had a firm ally in President Trump. The president defended Mr. Huang all week and praised him again on Thursday for doing a “fantastic job”; Mr. Trump then recommended that Tim Cook, the former Apple chief executive, take the helm at Nvidia. A series of reports by The New York Times showed that Mr. Huang, 63, had a relationship with Alice Huang, a Chinese businesswoman who had been recruited by China’s main spy agency to gather information on Mr. Huang. The Times also reported that Mr. Trump had been warned about the relationship but took no action. U.S. officials suspect that Megaspeed, the Singaporean company where Ms. Huang was a top executive, has helped to smuggle restricted chips into China. Ms. Huang has not responded to requests for comment; China has rejected the espionage claims and called the smuggling allegations “smears.” On Capitol Hill, Democrats called for an investigation into whether Mr. Huang had compromised U.S. national security. Senator Chuck Schumer of New York, the minority leader, said the Trump administration also “must answer for what it did once it learned about Mr. Huang’s relationship with a suspected Chinese intelligence asset.” Senator John Thune, Republican of South Dakota and the majority leader, said on Thursday that he anticipated Mr. Huang’s resignation would not keep Congress from conducting hearings on his relationship with a suspected Chinese spy. “It would make sense because of the nature of the association,” he said. Nvidia’s board : The board did not mention Mr. Huang’s conduct in its statement announcing his resignation. Instead, it thanked him for his “immeasurable contributions to the company and the industry.” Colette Kress, Nvidia’s chief financial officer , will serve as interim chief executive while the search for a permanent replacement is carried out, it said. Another affair: Mr. Huang had a second extramarital relationship with an executive who reported to him, according to five people who worked at the company, The Times reported on Wednesday. He is the latest member to join a growing club of chief executives brought down by affairs. A long-term strategy: China’s intelligence services have for decades used romantic entanglements to compromise or extract information from prominent people. Although the use of seduction in espionage is not unique to China, the country’s use of it differs in the amount of time it is willing to invest. Read more › Mr. Huang resigned as Nvidia’s chief executive on Thursday. But that has not appeared to slow a bipartisan push for more information on whether he had compromised national security. Senator Chuck Schumer of New York, the Democratic leader, said in a social media post that Congress must “demand answers” from Mr. Huang. Mr. Schumer also called on the Trump administration to “answer for what it did once it learned about Mr. Huang’s relationship with a suspected Chinese intelligence asset.” Mr. Lutnick’s department was required to review companies for national security risks before the Trump administration allowed Nvidia to sell advanced chips to China last year. The top Democrats on two congressional committees also wrote to Mr. Lutnick on Thursday, saying they were investigating the matter. My colleagues and I went on Hard Fork, the New York Times podcast about the future of technology, to discuss Jensen Huang’s resignation and its impact on the global tech industry. Listen to or watch it here . House Republicans said they were in discussions with Jensen Huang to get him to testify before Congress sometime this month. Representatives Brian Mast of Florida, who leads the Foreign Affairs Committee, and John Mooelnar of Michigan, who leads a different House committee focused on China, separately told reporters that they had been working to confirm a date and format for Huang to discuss allegations that he had an affair with a woman who U.S. intelligence agencies have concluded was spying for China. Huang’s testimony is not yet scheduled, and it is not clear whether his testimony would be public. Nvidia shares recovered most of their losses in the market by the close of trading, finishing more than 4 percent lower. The stock had fallen by as much as 14 percent Thursday morning after the resignation of Jensen Huang was announced. But as investors’ fears about the company’s future without Huang eased, the shares rebounded. Jensen Huang’s resignation may take down another victim: the movement to build open source A.I. systems, according to a report from SemiAnalysis, a prominent A.I. research group. Huang has been a champion for developing A.I. systems with public underlying code that are cheaper to run. The most advanced open source systems have been developed in China, using Nvidia chips, SemiAnalysis said. The U.S. open source ecosystem, as well as many American start-ups, rely on those Chinese models. “This is significantly impaired with Jensen gone,” the analysts wrote. Senator John Thune, Republican of South Dakota and the majority leader, told reporters at the Capitol on Thursday that he anticipated Congress would conduct oversight into Jensen Huang’s apparent involvement with an alleged Chinese spy, even though Huang has resigned as chief executive of Nvidia. “It would make sense because of the nature of the association,” he said. The Democratic leader, Senator Chuck Schumer of New York, said in a social media post that Congress must “demand answers” from Huang and Nvidia officials about “how they may have put U.S. national security at risk.” He added the Trump administration “must answer for what it did once it learned about Mr. Huang’s relationship with a suspected Chinese intelligence asset.” Over the past week, some of Silicon Valley’s most influential investors had argued that America could not win the A.I. race without Jensen Huang, casting his relationship with a woman believed to be a Chinese spy as a personal lapse that should be forgiven because of his importance to the industry. Some kept making that argument even after The New York Times reported Wednesday that Huang also had a relationship with an Nvidia executive who reports to him, hours before his resignation. “Sadly, greatness doesn’t guarantee goodness,” Sarah Guo, a venture capitalist, wrote on X late Wednesday. On Thursday, she called his resignation “a big loss.” Theodore Schleifer writes about philanthropy. Jensen Huang was just becoming one of America’s biggest philanthropists before his departure as the chief executive of Nvidia. With an estimated net worth of about $145 billion , he and his wife, Lori, had built one of the country’s largest foundations, with about $9 billion in assets. But Mr. Huang said this week that he had been unfaithful to his wife, acknowledging an affair with a woman U.S. intelligence has determined was a Chinese spy. The Times then reported that he had another affair with an Nvidia executive who reports to him. Nvidia said on Thursday morning that Mr. Huang was resigning from the company he had led for 33 years. Jensen Huang is by far the largest shareholder in Nvidia, holding a 3.56 percent stake, making him one of the wealthiest people in the world. But he does not have voting power like some of Silicon Valley’s other chief executives, such as Meta’s Mark Zuckerberg. That power — which usually comes from “super voting” shares — can shield chief executives from activist investors, market pressures and the board itself. “If the C.E.O. doesn’t do his job according to 12 or 15 board members, the C.E.O. is let go,” Huang said on a podcast in January. But he added, “there will never be one like me, and the reason for that is because I was raised by the company.” Its loan commitments and financing arrangements would make Nvidia the 10th largest bank in the country, according to an estimate from Ryan Cummings, the chief of staff for the Stanford Institute for Economic Policy Research. “Nvidia is at the center of this circular financing, and obviously at the center of Nvidia is Jensen Huang,” Mr. Cummings said. “He has been the driving force, pretty inarguably, behind a lot of the A.I. build-out.” Without Mr. Huang in charge, Nvidia’s role could change, Mr. Cummings said. And while it is possible that other companies will step in to fill the gap, that isn’t guaranteed. The appointment of Colette Kress, who has been Nvidia’s chief financial officer, to lead the company on an interim basis will likely raise questions in Washington about how much she was aware of the company’s dealings with Megaspeed, the Singaporean data center firm that was led by the alleged Chinese spy with whom Jensen Huang had an affair. Late last year, as U.S. government concerns were rising about Megaspeed, Nvidia suddenly changed how it recorded its global revenue, making it harder to see how much of its sales were being booked through Southeast Asia and Singapore. It also remains to be seen what Kress’s attitude will be toward issues like alleged chip smuggling and export controls. October 2026: Mr. Huang’s affair with Ms. Huang is reported in The New York Times . November 2026: After Mr. Huang admits the affair, Nvidia’s board says it will conduct an investigation. The New York Times later reports that Mr. Huang also had a relationship with Kimberly Powell , Nvidia’s vice president of health care, who reports to him. On Nov. 12, Nvidia’s board of directors announces that Mr. Huang has resigned . President Trump has been curiously silent about this since we and others reported that the Nvidia board was assessing Jensen Huang’s fate. Trump and Huang had developed a close relationship . Among global tech executives, few have had as much sway as Huang over Trump’s approach to A.I. and China.

Mr. Huang, the co-founder and chief executive of the Silicon Valley chip giant, stepped down after Nvidia’s board started an inquiry into allegations that he had extramarital affairs with a woman who U.S. intelligence agencies have concluded was spying for China, as well as with an executive who reported to him.

It was the stunning fall of one of the most powerful figures in the A.I. boom. Nvidia controls an estimated 90 percent of the market for the advanced chips that are an essential component of artificial intelligence projects.

It also touched the White House, where Mr. Huang long had a firm ally in President Trump. The president defended Mr. Huang all week and praised him again on Thursday for doing a “fantastic job”; Mr. Trump then recommended that Tim Cook, the former Apple chief executive, take the helm at Nvidia.

A series of reports by The New York Times showed that Mr. Huang, 63, had a relationship with Alice Huang, a Chinese businesswoman who had been recruited by China’s main spy agency to gather information on Mr. Huang. The Times also reported that Mr. Trump had been warned about the relationship but took no action.

U.S. officials suspect that Megaspeed, the Singaporean company where Ms. Huang was a top executive, has helped to smuggle restricted chips into China. Ms. Huang has not responded to requests for comment; China has rejected the espionage claims and called the smuggling allegations “smears.”

On Capitol Hill, Democrats called for an investigation into whether Mr. Huang had compromised U.S. national security. Senator Chuck Schumer of New York, the minority leader, said the Trump administration also “must answer for what it did once it learned about Mr. Huang’s relationship with a suspected Chinese intelligence asset.”

Senator John Thune, Republican of South Dakota and the majority leader, said on Thursday that he anticipated Mr. Huang’s resignation would not keep Congress from conducting hearings on his relationship with a suspected Chinese spy. “It would make sense because of the nature of the association,” he said.

Nvidia’s board : The board did not mention Mr. Huang’s conduct in its statement announcing his resignation. Instead, it thanked him for his “immeasurable contributions to the company and the industry.” Colette Kress, Nvidia’s chief financial officer , will serve as interim chief executive while the search for a permanent replacement is carried out, it said.

Another affair: Mr. Huang had a second extramarital relationship with an executive who reported to him, according to five people who worked at the company, The Times reported on Wednesday. He is the latest member to join a growing club of chief executives brought down by affairs.

A long-term strategy: China’s intelligence services have for decades used romantic entanglements to compromise or extract information from prominent people. Although the use of seduction in espionage is not unique to China, the country’s use of it differs in the amount of time it is willing to invest. Read more ›
Mr. Huang resigned as Nvidia’s chief executive on Thursday. But that has not appeared to slow a bipartisan push for more information on whether he had compromised national security.

Senator Chuck Schumer of New York, the Democratic leader, said in a social media post that Congress must “demand answers” from Mr. Huang. Mr. Schumer also called on the Trump administration to “answer for what it did once it learned about Mr. Huang’s relationship with a suspected Chinese intelligence asset.”

Mr. Lutnick’s department was required to review companies for national security risks before the Trump administration allowed Nvidia to sell advanced chips to China last year. The top Democrats on two congressional committees also wrote to Mr. Lutnick on Thursday, saying they were investigating the matter.

My colleagues and I went on Hard Fork, the New York Times podcast about the future of technology, to discuss Jensen Huang’s resignation and its impact on the global tech industry. Listen to or watch it here .

House Republicans said they were in discussions with Jensen Huang to get him to testify before Congress sometime this month. Representatives Brian Mast of Florida, who leads the Foreign Affairs Committee, and John Mooelnar of Michigan, who leads a different House committee focused on China, separately told reporters that they had been working to confirm a date and format for Huang to discuss allegations that he had an affair with a woman who U.S. intelligence agencies have concluded was spying for China.
Huang’s testimony is not yet scheduled, and it is not clear whether his testimony would be public.

Nvidia shares recovered most of their losses in the market by the close of trading, finishing more than 4 percent lower. The stock had fallen by as much as 14 percent Thursday morning after the resignation of Jensen Huang was announced. But as investors’ fears about the company’s future without Huang eased, the shares rebounded.

Jensen Huang’s resignation may take down another victim: the movement to build open source A.I. systems, according to a report from SemiAnalysis, a prominent A.I. research group. Huang has been a champion for developing A.I. systems with public underlying code that are cheaper to run.

The most advanced open source systems have been developed in China, using Nvidia chips, SemiAnalysis said. The U.S. open source ecosystem, as well as many American start-ups, rely on those Chinese models. “This is significantly impaired with Jensen gone,” the analysts wrote.

Senator John Thune, Republican of South Dakota and the majority leader, told reporters at the Capitol on Thursday that he anticipated Congress would conduct oversight into Jensen Huang’s apparent involvement with an alleged Chinese spy, even though Huang has resigned as chief executive of Nvidia. “It would make sense because of the nature of the association,” he said.

The Democratic leader, Senator Chuck Schumer of New York, said in a social media post that Congress must “demand answers” from Huang and Nvidia officials about “how they may have put U.S. national security at risk.” He added the Trump administration “must answer for what it did once it learned about Mr. Huang’s relationship with a suspected Chinese intelligence asset.”

Over the past week, some of Silicon Valley’s most influential investors had argued that America could not win the A.I. race without Jensen Huang, casting his relationship with a woman believed to be a Chinese spy as a personal lapse that should be forgiven because of his importance to the industry. Some kept making that argument even after The New York Times reported Wednesday that Huang also had a relationship with an Nvidia executive who reports to him, hours before his resignation. “Sadly, greatness doesn’t guarantee goodness,” Sarah Guo, a venture capitalist, wrote on X late Wednesday. On Thursday, she called his resignation “a big loss.”
Theodore Schleifer writes about philanthropy.

Jensen Huang was just becoming one of America’s biggest philanthropists before his departure as the chief executive of Nvidia. With an estimated net worth of about $145 billion , he and his wife, Lori, had built one of the country’s largest foundations, with about $9 billion in assets.

But Mr. Huang said this week that he had been unfaithful to his wife, acknowledging an affair with a woman U.S. intelligence has determined was a Chinese spy. The Times then reported that he had another affair with an Nvidia executive who reports to him. Nvidia said on Thursday morning that Mr. Huang was resigning from the company he had led for 33 years.

Jensen Huang is by far the largest shareholder in Nvidia, holding a 3.56 percent stake, making him one of the wealthiest people in the world. But he does not have voting power like some of Silicon Valley’s other chief executives, such as Meta’s Mark Zuckerberg. That power — which usually comes from “super voting” shares — can shield chief executives from activist investors, market pressures and the board itself.

“If the C.E.O. doesn’t do his job according to 12 or 15 board members, the C.E.O. is let go,” Huang said on a podcast in January. But he added, “there will never be one like me, and the reason for that is because I was raised by the company.”

Its loan commitments and financing arrangements would make Nvidia the 10th largest bank in the country, according to an estimate from Ryan Cummings, the chief of staff for the Stanford Institute for Economic Policy Research.

“Nvidia is at the center of this circular financing, and obviously at the center of Nvidia is Jensen Huang,” Mr. Cummings said. “He has been the driving force, pretty inarguably, behind a lot of the A.I. build-out.”
Without Mr. Huang in charge, Nvidia’s role could change, Mr. Cummings said. And while it is possible that other companies will step in to fill the gap, that isn’t guaranteed.

The appointment of Colette Kress, who has been Nvidia’s chief financial officer, to lead the company on an interim basis will likely raise questions in Washington about how much she was aware of the company’s dealings with Megaspeed, the Singaporean data center firm that was led by the alleged Chinese spy with whom Jensen Huang had an affair.

Late last year, as U.S. government concerns were rising about Megaspeed, Nvidia suddenly changed how it recorded its global revenue, making it harder to see how much of its sales were being booked through Southeast Asia and Singapore. It also remains to be seen what Kress’s attitude will be toward issues like alleged chip smuggling and export controls.

The New York Times later reports that Mr. Huang also had a relationship with Kimberly Powell , Nvidia’s vice president of health care, who reports to him. On Nov. 12, Nvidia’s board of directors announces that Mr. Huang has resigned .

President Trump has been curiously silent about this since we and others reported that the Nvidia board was assessing Jensen Huang’s fate. Trump and Huang had developed a close relationship . Among global tech executives, few have had as much sway as Huang over Trump’s approach to A.I. and China.

Colette Kress , the current executive vice president and chief financial officer, has agreed to take over as interim CEO, the company said in a statement . "The Board has full confidence in Colette and the leadership team, and we expect the company’s operations, customer commitments and product roadmap to continue without interruption," said Harvey Jones, chair of the Nvidia Board of Directors. The Nvidia board is launching a search for a permanent CEO, and it will consider both applicants from within and outside the company, the statement said. Shares of Nvidia tumbled about 5% as of Thursday morning, recovering some of the losses from a plunge of more than 13% at the open of trading. Huang's resignation came days after the company issued a statement announcing an investigation into Huang in light of reporting he "has been the target of a foreign intelligence effort." He later admitted in an internal message to Nvidia staff that he had been "unfaithful to his wife." Amid the fallout from the allegations and the internal message, The New York Times reported on Wednesday that Huang also allegedly had an extramarital relationship with an Nvidia executive who allegedly reports to him. The outlet, citing sources within the company, reported that Huang and his colleague were allegedly captured on video being affectionate at a hotel during an Nvidia conference in March. The Times said it had not seen the video. ABC News has not been able to verify the reporting or the alleged video. Following the reporting about Jensen Huang and Alice Huang, who are not related, the Chinese government denied the allegations, calling them "baseless and purely slanderous smears against China." Neither Alice Huang nor her employer, Megaspeed International, responded to ABC News' request for comment after the Times story broke. Alice Huang is currently living in China, Bloomberg reported on Wednesday. Nvidia soared to prominence in recent years by selling most of the advanced chips behind the AI boom. The company has defied skeptics with strong revenue quarter after quarter, despite political backlash against data centers and looming concerns about an AI financial bubble. While the stock has performed well over a long-term period it has struggled to keep rising at a steady clip of late, even before the scandal surrounding Huang. Shares of Nvidia are up a staggering 429% over the past five years, even though the stock has fallen about 17% compared to a year ago. As of Thursday morning, Nvidia ranked as the third-largest public company in the world as measured by market capitalization. The two larger public companies are Apple and Microsoft. On Sunday, Nvidia shared with ABC News the internal message Jensen Huang sent to employees, in which he said he was "unfaithful," apologizing for hurting his wife and family. extraction.body: The abrupt resignation of Nvidia’s chief executive, Jensen Huang, on Thursday morning after revelations that he had extramarital affairs with two women sent shock waves through the A.I. industry and spurred calls on Capitol Hill for investigations into whether U.S. security had been compromised. Mr. Huang, the co-founder and chief executive of the Silicon Valley chip giant, stepped down after Nvidia’s board started an inquiry into allegations that he had extramarital affairs with a woman who U.S. intelligence agencies have concluded was spying for China, as well as with an executive who reported to him. It was the stunning fall of one of the most powerful figures in the A.I. boom. Nvidia controls an estimated 90 percent of the market for the advanced chips that are an essential component of artificial intelligence projects. It also touched the White House, where Mr. Huang long had a firm ally in President Trump. The president defended Mr. Huang all week and praised him again on Thursday for doing a “fantastic job”; Mr. Trump then recommended that Tim Cook, the former Apple chief executive, take the helm at Nvidia. A series of reports by The New York Times showed that Mr. Huang, 63, had a relationship with Alice Huang, a Chinese businesswoman who had been recruited by China’s main spy agency to gather information on Mr. Huang. The Times also reported that Mr. Trump had been warned about the relationship but took no action. U.S. officials suspect that Megaspeed, the Singaporean company where Ms. Huang was a top executive, has helped to smuggle restricted chips into China. Ms. Huang has not responded to requests for comment; China has rejected the espionage claims and called the smuggling allegations “smears.” Nvidia’s board : The board did not mention Mr. Huang’s conduct in its statement announcing his resignation. Instead, it thanked him for his “immeasurable contributions to the company and the industry.” Colette Kress, Nvidia’s chief financial officer , will serve as interim chief executive while the search for a permanent replacement is carried out, it said. Another affair: Mr. Huang had a second extramarital relationship with an executive who reported to him, according to five people who worked at the company, The Times reported on Wednesday. He is the latest member to join a growing club of chief executives brought down by affairs. A long-term strategy: China’s intelligence services have for decades used romantic entanglements to compromise or extract information from prominent people. extraction.body: A romantic relationship between a CEO and a vice president who reports directly to him could create a serious conflict of interest. When that relationship is allegedly undisclosed and the executive holds authority over the subordinate's career, compensation, and responsibilities, it becomes a governance problem , not a personal one. The New York Times, citing five people who worked at Nvidia and spoke anonymously, reported that Jensen Huang allegedly had an extramarital relationship with Kimberly Powell, Nvidia's vice president of health care, who reportedly reports to him. Both Huang and Powell are married to other people, according to the Times. Two of the five anonymous sources told the Times that Huang and Powell were captured on video appearing affectionate at a San Jose hotel during Nvidia's GTC developer conference in March. The Times stated it had not viewed the video, and its existence should not be treated as established. The responses from all three parties were notable mostly for what they were not. Nvidia declined to comment to the Times. Powell did not respond to a request for comment. When the Times reached Huang directly, he said "I don't think you should be talking to me directly" and ended the call. Huang did not expressly deny the allegation in that exchange. This allegation is distinct from the separate matter in which Huang acknowledged being unfaithful to his wife in a message to Nvidia employees, according to the BBC. That admission concerned a different alleged relationship, with Alice Huang. U.S. officials reportedly assessed Alice Huang to be a Chinese intelligence asset , an assessment China has denied. Nvidia's board retained Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen and Katz to conduct an independent investigation into that matter, according to CNBC. Whether the scope of that investigation covers the Powell allegation is not public. Nvidia's own code of conduct, as characterized in Times reporting, instructs employees to avoid situations that create conflicts of interest, including those involving personal relationships, and states that the company investigates misconduct reports promptly. A reporting relationship between a CEO and a vice president is exactly what those rules exist to prevent. The available evidence does not confirm whether Nvidia's policies include explicit provisions for the chief executive, but the conflict-of-interest framework applies broadly to the company's workforce. The allegation and the footage described by anonymous sources both remain without independent confirmation. Whether the alleged relationship affected Powell's career trajectory, pay, or responsibilities at Nvidia has not been publicly confirmed. Powell joined Nvidia in 2008 and advanced to vice president of government health care after earlier roles in AI business development . No reporting establishes a connection between that progression and the alleged relationship. Nvidia shares fell more than 3% in after-hours trading after the Times published its report, according to CNBC, though that decline likely reflects the cumulative weight of multiple ongoing concerns. The more consequential question is not on a stock ticker. Five people inside Nvidia allegedly knew enough about a reported relationship between the CEO and a direct report to speak with a reporter. Whether any internal process addressed that situation before a law firm was retained for a separate investigation is not established by the available reporting. Nvidia's board faces a governance structure that was not built to scrutinize the person who built the company, and that gap is exactly what an independent review should now examine.

Other large corporations have made similar announcements recently, including Bank of America, which cautioned users last week to never share user IDs and passwords with agents. Many companies, particularly banks and airlines, have faced mounting difficulty as they try to separate human customers from their AI assistants. The firms warn that consumers’ credentials are at risk of leaking when they entrust agents with their logins and passwords. “Sharing account credentials with personal, third-party, AI assistants can expose sensitive information, and actions taken by these tools may result in unintended purchases, account changes, or use of MileagePlus miles,” United said in a Wednesday press release . Automated AI actions also could break Federal Aviation Administration and Department of Transportation rules, the release said, citing the fact that flight check-in requires “human acknowledgment that bags do not contain banned substances like explosives.” The airline is implementing the new access restrictions both within its own digital platforms and separately through aggregators and agencies. “This work includes updates to our booking, ticketing and distribution policies,” the press release said. The airline is the latest American corporate giant to prevent customers from using AI agents and autonomous assistants to access their systems. The move comes as airlines and banks are struggling to differentiate between real customers and AI systems operating on their behalf, such as when users share their logins with their AI assistants. Sharing passwords with apps and assistants can create security risks if those credentials get leaked or exposed. United warns that “sharing account credentials with personal, third-party, AI assistants can expose sensitive information, and actions taken by these tools may result in unintended purchases, account changes, or use of MileagePlus miles.” The airline also warns of a risk of violating federal aviation rules, such as requiring that a human completes flight check-ins to acknowledge that their bags do not contain banned substances. “As a result, United is taking steps to restrict access — directly within our digital platforms and indirectly via travel agencies and aggregators — to prohibit use by unauthorized, third-party personal AI agents or assistants,” the airline said in a statement . “This work includes updates to our booking, ticketing and distribution policies.” The airline’s move follows a warning from banks, including Bank of America, which last week urged customers not to share their passwords with their AI assistants.

extraction.body: Amazon Web Services, a leader in the cloud infrastructure market, reported a major outage on Monday that took down numerous major websites. Many sites came back online within a few hours, although Downdetector showed another spike in user reports around noon ET of outages at Amazon, AWS and Alexa. The company's latest update at 6:53 p.m. ET noted that "all AWS services returned to normal operations" shortly after 6 p.m. ET. Some services continue to have a backlog of messages that will finish processing in the next few hours, AWS said. "We will share a detailed AWS post-event summary," the company said in the note. The update came after outages and delays persisted into Monday afternoon, with the company observing "increased error rates" for customers when trying to launch new instances in EC2, its popular cloud service that provides virtual server capacity. "We are working to fully restore service as quickly as possible," the company wrote at the time. Around 1:30 p.m. ET, AWS said it was starting to see "early signs" of EC2 recovery in some regions and that it was applying fixes to remaining areas "at which point we expect launch errors and network connectivity issues to subside." Amazon also confirmed that the outage impacted Amazon.com, some of its subsidiaries and AWS customer support operations. The outage was first reported at 3:11 a.m. ET in AWS' main US-East-1 region hosted in northern Virginia. A notice on AWS' status page said it was experiencing DNS problems with DynamoDB, its database service that underpins many other AWS applications. DNS, or Domain Name System, translates website names to IP addresses so browsers and other applications can load. AWS cited an "operational issue" affecting multiple services and said it was "working on multiple parallel paths to accelerate recovery," in an update at 5:01 a.m. ET. More than 70 of its own services were affected. AWS said in an update at 6:35 a.m. ET that the DNS issue had been "fully mitigated" and that AWS service operations were "succeeding normally." AWS is the leading provider of cloud infrastructure technology, accounting for around a third of the market, ahead of Microsoft and Google, according to Synergy Research Group . Millions of companies and organizations rely on AWS for cloud computing services, such as servers and storage. Downdetector showed user reports indicating problems at sites including Disney+ , Lyft , the McDonald's app, The New York Times , Reddit , Ring doorbells, Robinhood, Snapchat , United Airlines , T-Mobile and Venmo. British government websites Gov.uk and HM Revenue and Customs were also experiencing issues, per Downdetector. A government spokesperson told CNBC: "We are aware of an incident affecting Amazon Web Services, and several online services which rely on their infrastructure. Through our established incident response arrangements, we are in contact with the company, who are working to restore services as quickly as possible." Lloyds Banking Group confirmed that some of its services were affected and asked customers "to bear with us" while it worked to restore them. Some 20 minutes later, it added that services were coming back online. The outage also brought down critical tools inside Amazon. Warehouse and delivery employees, along with drivers for Amazon's Flex service, reported on Reddit that internal systems were offline at many sites. Some warehouse workers were instructed to stand by in break rooms and loading areas during their shift, while they couldn't load Amazon's Anytime Pay app, which lets employees access a portion of their paycheck immediately. Seller Central, the hub used by Amazon's third-party sellers to manage their businesses, was also knocked offline by the outage. Reddit, too, is "working on scaling Reddit back to 100 percent as we speak," a spokesperson told CNBC. Some United and Delta Air Lines customers reported on social media that they couldn't find their reservations online, check in or drop bags . A T-Mobile spokesperson said its customers had issues when trying to use other sites or services due to the AWS disruption, but that there "was no outage or service disruption" at the carrier. Canvas, an online teaching platform used to host course information and submit assignments, said it was also hit by the "ongoing AWS incident." Other social media users cited disruption across cloud-based games, including Roblox and Fortnite, while crypto exchange Coinbase said many users were unable to access the service due to the outage. Graphic design tool Canva said it was "experiencing significantly increased error rates which are impacting functionality on Canva. There is a major issue with our underlying cloud provider." Generative artificial intelligence search tool Perplexity was also affected. "The root cause is an AWS issue. We're working on resolving it," CEO Aravind Srinivas said in a post on X. It's not the first time in recent history that major companies have been affected by a technical issue. In July 2024, a faulty software upgrade by cybersecurity firm Crowdstrike revealed the fragility of global technology infrastructure when it caused Microsoft Windows systems to go dark, creating millions of dollars worth of chaos and grounding thousands of flights in the process. It also affected hospitals and banks. AWS has also experienced other outages in recent years. A disruption in 2023 knocked many websites offline for several hours, while a more severe outage in 2021 affected websites and services across the globe, including some of Amazon's own delivery operations, which were briefly brought to a standstill. Amazon, Microsoft and Google have long jockeyed to claim enterprise customers. After an outage of Microsoft's suite of productivity software earlier this month, Google sought to capitalize on the service lapse by pitching its own tools and a business continuity plan that runs its Workspace service in parallel with Microsoft 365. In a blog post last week, Google wrote, "Just because Microsoft 365 goes down -- and it's a question of when and for how long, not if -- doesn't mean that your teams need to go back to using pen and paper." Google's cloud services went down for an extended period in June, disrupting several major service providers like OpenAI and Shopify. The company said the outage was caused by multiple layers of flawed recent updates. Monday's AWS outage doesn't appear to have been caused by a cyberattack, but is more likely a "technical fault affecting one of Amazon's main data centres," Rob Jardin, chief digital officer at cybersecurity company NymVPN, said in a statement. "These issues can happen when systems become overloaded or a key part of the network goes down, and because so many websites and apps rely on AWS, the impact spreads quickly," he added. "This episode serves as a reminder of how dependent the world is on a handful of major cloud service providers: Amazon, Microsoft, and Google. When a major cloud provider sneezes, the Internet catches a cold." — CNBC's Leslie Josephs and Jennifer Elias contributed to this report.

sources.title: Microsoft IT outage: Global services slowly recovering after bug causes chaos - BBC
passages: Businesses and services around the world are slowly recovering after a massive IT outage affected computer systems for hours on Thursday and Friday.
The global chaos has sparked concern over the vulnerability of the world's interconnected technologies, and the extent to which a single software glitch could have such widespread impact.
sources.body: Businesses and services around the world are slowly recovering after a massive IT outage affected computer systems for hours on Thursday and Friday. The global chaos has sparked concern over the vulnerability of the world's interconnected technologies, and the extent to which a single software glitch could have such widespread impact.

extraction.body: Businesses and services around the world are slowly recovering after a massive IT outage affected computer systems for hours on Thursday and Friday. Businesses, banks, hospitals and airlines were among the worst-hit after cyber-security firm CrowdStrike issued a faulty software update which affected Microsoft Windows. CrowdStrike's CEO apologised for the disruption and said a fix had been issued, but admitted it could be "some time" before all systems were back up and running. While some airline services are beginning to return to normal after thousands of flights were cancelled, operators expect some delays and cancellations to persist through the weekend. Many businesses are now dealing with backlogs and missed orders that could take days to resolve. Health services in Britain, Israel and Germany also suffered problems, with some operations cancelled. The global chaos has sparked concern over the vulnerability of the world's interconnected technologies, and the extent to which a single software glitch could have such widespread impact. The issue began at 19:00 GMT on Thursday, affecting Windows users running cybersecurity software CrowdStrike Falcon, according to Microsoft, though the full extent of the problem only became clear by Friday morning. But by Friday evening, the problems were easing in many parts of the globe, with many airports saying that while there were still issues with check-in and payment systems, most flights were now running. Hong Kong International Airport has resumed normal operations, according to Chinese state media. Meanwhile, JP Morgan Chase, the biggest bank in the US, said it is working to restore service to ATM machines. The website Downdetector, which detects sites which may be having tech issues, showed fewer sites in the UK which were experiencing problems by the end of the day. CrowdStrike CEO George Kurtz said on X that a defect was found "in a single content update for Windows hosts". "We're deeply sorry for the impact that we've caused to customers, to travellers, to anyone affected by this, including our company," he told the NBC network. "Many of the customers are rebooting the system and it's coming up and it'll be operational. "It could be some time for some systems that just automatically won't recover, but it is our mission... to make sure every customer is fully recovered." Microsoft has also said that several reboots may be required, with some users reporting that as many as 15 could be needed before the problem is fixed. Also, tech experts say CrowdStrike's fix will have to be applied separately to each and every device affected. By 18:00 GMT, aviation data from Cirium suggested that more than 4,000 flights - or 3.9% of the total - had been cancelled so far on Friday, though the figure may also include flights cancelled for other reasons. Payment systems, banking and healthcare providers around the world were affected. It is thought the outage may also have a longer term effect as companies struggle to pay wages to staff, particularly where payments are made on a weekly basis. Some railway companies warned of delays, and broadcasters Sky News and ABC Australia both experienced outages.

The extent of the outage wasn’t clear but the company said in January that it had more than 450 million paid Microsoft 365 commercial subscriptions. The company indicated that its recovery efforts were making progress Friday, saying it was “seeing encouraging recovery progress, with service availability and email delivery performance improving across a growing portion of affected Microsoft 365 infrastructure." Though the company cautioned "some users may still experience intermittent issues as recovery actions continue." But problems appeared to persist, according to an outage tracking site, status reports from organizations that depend on the company's services and anecdotal reports on social media. The Redmond, Washington-based company said it was trying different ways to identify the cause of the problem and get its servers back online, using “a measured approach to identify and repair affected infrastructure.” The company said it did not have any indication that the outage was caused by malicious activity and would treat the incident “with urgency and priority until full resolution.” A series of posts by the company on X suggested its engineers were struggling to get the problem fully under control. Hours after saying it managed to successfully restore service health and functionality, the company said it had updated its list of impacted services and was continuing to address the issue. An earlier post offered little hope for users expecting a quick resolution. “We’ve monitored the status of the changes applied to improve serviceability and confirmed they’re not taking as expected,” the company wrote. In a pair of more recent updates on Friday, Microsoft said “we’re seeing early stabilization and capacity improvements as recovery actions continue.” “Recovery actions are ongoing across affected Microsoft 365 infrastructure and progressing in phases,” the company said in a second post. “We’re seeing incremental improvement in several workloads, but service health remains variable and capacity has not yet fully returned to baseline.” U.S.-based industrial technology company Workhorse Group Inc. delayed a conference call for its quarterly earnings because of the outage. In Australia, Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke said Friday Microsoft had likened the widespread outage to the CrowdStrike outage in 2024. Burke said he had spoken to Microsoft’s top executive in Australia and the government’s national cybersecurity coordinator about the global disruption. They believe that they are dealing in some ways (with something) similar to what we saw with respect to CrowdStrike where there is an update that has gone awry,” Burke told reporters in Sydney. Hong Kong businessperson Danny Lau, who runs an aluminum firm, said his company's Outlook accounts could not receive updates from their U.S. customers due to the outage. If the situation dragged on further, this could “impact the production timeline,” he said. Some banks in Hong Kong, an Asian financial hub, also saw part of their operations disrupted. Air India said its flight operations were unaffected by the global Microsoft outage. However, it temporarily rerouted its email services to ensure customer queries continued to reach the airline without interruption, the company said in a statement. IndiGo, another Indian airline company, said it also reported disruptions to its email support services, which affected its ability to receive customer queries. The airline in a statement on X said its other support channels remained operational and its flight operations were unaffected. Singapore’s Government Technology Agency said that government emails were down and that the agency is working with Microsoft to resolve the issue. The Philippines' Supreme Court said in a statement on X that the ongoing Microsoft 365 service outage has affected some of its operations, including email responses. In Japan , Deputy Chief Cabinet Secretary Masanao Ozaki said the outage impacted the government’s IT infrastructure and that they were “keeping a close eye on the developments.” Japanese authorities had taken steps including securing alternative communication tools such as telephones, the government said. passages: Schools, councils and other organisations across Northern Ireland are among those impacted by a global Microsoft outage.
Microsoft 365 is also used by companies worldwide and is expected to have a knock-on effect to other services.
In a statement Lisburn and Castlereagh City Council said they are aware of the "ongoing global disruption" and will share "further updates if necessary".
Microsoft 365 Services, including Teams, Outlook and Microsoft's artificial intelligence software Copilot, have been affected by "connectivity problems".
