extraction.body: Schools, councils and other organisations across Northern Ireland are among those impacted by a global Microsoft outage. Problems with the software giant started on Thursday, with monitoring website Downdetector seeing problems reported in more than 70 countries. Microsoft has said it is seeing "encouraging recovery progress" in Europe, and North America is "improving", but adds "some users may still experience intermittent issues". Earlier, it said the issue wasn't caused by a cyber-security breach Public bodies such as the Education Authority said on Friday: "Outlook is currently unavailable to NI schools and the Education Authority. Emails cannot currently be sent or received." The South Eastern Health Trust said there will be "no impact on clinical services". Northern Ireland Ambulance Service said that patient services are not impacted by the outage. Some councils in Northern Ireland have said that their emails systems have been impacted. Belfast City Council said it is experiencing issues "receiving and responding" to emails. "Our website and phone lines are operating as normal however, and customers can still log requests." In a statement Lisburn and Castlereagh City Council said they are aware of the "ongoing global disruption" and will share "further updates if necessary". Causeway Coast and Glens Borough Council confirmed they have been impacted and said the majority of council services are unaffected however there is disruption to staff's ability to send and receive emails. Queen's University Belfast also said they are experiencing email disruption on Friday. "Our students and staff are currently unable to receive or send emails and may experience difficulties accessing. "As always, staff and students should not use personal email accounts to send, receive or store university-related communications or information." The Police Service of Northern Ireland have issued a statement to say its services are unaffected. Microsoft 365 Services, including Teams, Outlook and Microsoft's artificial intelligence software Copilot, have been affected by "connectivity problems". Customers are reporting varying levels of access - many have not been able to send or receive emails, view certain files or details on their calendar apps. Some users have been able to use Teams and are using messaging and online meeting functions without issues. More than 430 million people use Microsoft 365 apps according to Microsoft's website. The full scale of the outage has not been confirmed, but monitoring website Downdetector had 140,000 people from 74 countries report issues with Outlook on Thursday evening. The real figure affected is likely much higher because Downdetector relies primarily on users self-reporting. Microsoft 365 is also used by companies worldwide and is expected to have a knock-on effect to other services.

extraction.body: Amazon Web Services, a leader in the cloud infrastructure market, reported a major outage on Monday that took down numerous major websites. Many sites came back online within a few hours, although Downdetector showed another spike in user reports around noon ET of outages at Amazon, AWS and Alexa. The company's latest update at 6:53 p.m. ET noted that "all AWS services returned to normal operations" shortly after 6 p.m. ET. Some services continue to have a backlog of messages that will finish processing in the next few hours, AWS said. "We will share a detailed AWS post-event summary," the company said in the note. The update came after outages and delays persisted into Monday afternoon, with the company observing "increased error rates" for customers when trying to launch new instances in EC2, its popular cloud service that provides virtual server capacity. "We are working to fully restore service as quickly as possible," the company wrote at the time. Around 1:30 p.m. ET, AWS said it was starting to see "early signs" of EC2 recovery in some regions and that it was applying fixes to remaining areas "at which point we expect launch errors and network connectivity issues to subside." Amazon also confirmed that the outage impacted Amazon.com, some of its subsidiaries and AWS customer support operations. The outage was first reported at 3:11 a.m. ET in AWS' main US-East-1 region hosted in northern Virginia. A notice on AWS' status page said it was experiencing DNS problems with DynamoDB, its database service that underpins many other AWS applications. DNS, or Domain Name System, translates website names to IP addresses so browsers and other applications can load. AWS cited an "operational issue" affecting multiple services and said it was "working on multiple parallel paths to accelerate recovery," in an update at 5:01 a.m. ET. More than 70 of its own services were affected. AWS said in an update at 6:35 a.m. ET that the DNS issue had been "fully mitigated" and that AWS service operations were "succeeding normally." AWS is the leading provider of cloud infrastructure technology, accounting for around a third of the market, ahead of Microsoft and Google, according to Synergy Research Group . Millions of companies and organizations rely on AWS for cloud computing services, such as servers and storage. Downdetector showed user reports indicating problems at sites including Disney+ , Lyft , the McDonald's app, The New York Times , Reddit , Ring doorbells, Robinhood, Snapchat , United Airlines , T-Mobile and Venmo. British government websites Gov.uk and HM Revenue and Customs were also experiencing issues, per Downdetector. A government spokesperson told CNBC: "We are aware of an incident affecting Amazon Web Services, and several online services which rely on their infrastructure. Through our established incident response arrangements, we are in contact with the company, who are working to restore services as quickly as possible." Lloyds Banking Group confirmed that some of its services were affected and asked customers "to bear with us" while it worked to restore them. Some 20 minutes later, it added that services were coming back online. The outage also brought down critical tools inside Amazon. Warehouse and delivery employees, along with drivers for Amazon's Flex service, reported on Reddit that internal systems were offline at many sites. Some warehouse workers were instructed to stand by in break rooms and loading areas during their shift, while they couldn't load Amazon's Anytime Pay app, which lets employees access a portion of their paycheck immediately. Seller Central, the hub used by Amazon's third-party sellers to manage their businesses, was also knocked offline by the outage. Reddit, too, is "working on scaling Reddit back to 100 percent as we speak," a spokesperson told CNBC. Some United and Delta Air Lines customers reported on social media that they couldn't find their reservations online, check in or drop bags . A T-Mobile spokesperson said its customers had issues when trying to use other sites or services due to the AWS disruption, but that there "was no outage or service disruption" at the carrier. Canvas, an online teaching platform used to host course information and submit assignments, said it was also hit by the "ongoing AWS incident." Other social media users cited disruption across cloud-based games, including Roblox and Fortnite, while crypto exchange Coinbase said many users were unable to access the service due to the outage. Graphic design tool Canva said it was "experiencing significantly increased error rates which are impacting functionality on Canva. There is a major issue with our underlying cloud provider." Generative artificial intelligence search tool Perplexity was also affected. "The root cause is an AWS issue. We're working on resolving it," CEO Aravind Srinivas said in a post on X. It's not the first time in recent history that major companies have been affected by a technical issue. In July 2024, a faulty software upgrade by cybersecurity firm Crowdstrike revealed the fragility of global technology infrastructure when it caused Microsoft Windows systems to go dark, creating millions of dollars worth of chaos and grounding thousands of flights in the process. It also affected hospitals and banks. AWS has also experienced other outages in recent years. A disruption in 2023 knocked many websites offline for several hours, while a more severe outage in 2021 affected websites and services across the globe, including some of Amazon's own delivery operations, which were briefly brought to a standstill. Amazon, Microsoft and Google have long jockeyed to claim enterprise customers. After an outage of Microsoft's suite of productivity software earlier this month, Google sought to capitalize on the service lapse by pitching its own tools and a business continuity plan that runs its Workspace service in parallel with Microsoft 365. In a blog post last week, Google wrote, "Just because Microsoft 365 goes down -- and it's a question of when and for how long, not if -- doesn't mean that your teams need to go back to using pen and paper." Google's cloud services went down for an extended period in June, disrupting several major service providers like OpenAI and Shopify. The company said the outage was caused by multiple layers of flawed recent updates. Monday's AWS outage doesn't appear to have been caused by a cyberattack, but is more likely a "technical fault affecting one of Amazon's main data centres," Rob Jardin, chief digital officer at cybersecurity company NymVPN, said in a statement. "These issues can happen when systems become overloaded or a key part of the network goes down, and because so many websites and apps rely on AWS, the impact spreads quickly," he added. "This episode serves as a reminder of how dependent the world is on a handful of major cloud service providers: Amazon, Microsoft, and Google. When a major cloud provider sneezes, the Internet catches a cold." — CNBC's Leslie Josephs and Jennifer Elias contributed to this report.

sources.title: Microsoft IT outage: Global services slowly recovering after bug causes chaos - BBC
passages: Businesses and services around the world are slowly recovering after a massive IT outage affected computer systems for hours on Thursday and Friday.
The global chaos has sparked concern over the vulnerability of the world's interconnected technologies, and the extent to which a single software glitch could have such widespread impact.
sources.body: Businesses and services around the world are slowly recovering after a massive IT outage affected computer systems for hours on Thursday and Friday. The global chaos has sparked concern over the vulnerability of the world's interconnected technologies, and the extent to which a single software glitch could have such widespread impact.

extraction.body: Businesses and services around the world are slowly recovering after a massive IT outage affected computer systems for hours on Thursday and Friday. Businesses, banks, hospitals and airlines were among the worst-hit after cyber-security firm CrowdStrike issued a faulty software update which affected Microsoft Windows. CrowdStrike's CEO apologised for the disruption and said a fix had been issued, but admitted it could be "some time" before all systems were back up and running. While some airline services are beginning to return to normal after thousands of flights were cancelled, operators expect some delays and cancellations to persist through the weekend. Many businesses are now dealing with backlogs and missed orders that could take days to resolve. Health services in Britain, Israel and Germany also suffered problems, with some operations cancelled. The global chaos has sparked concern over the vulnerability of the world's interconnected technologies, and the extent to which a single software glitch could have such widespread impact. The issue began at 19:00 GMT on Thursday, affecting Windows users running cybersecurity software CrowdStrike Falcon, according to Microsoft, though the full extent of the problem only became clear by Friday morning. But by Friday evening, the problems were easing in many parts of the globe, with many airports saying that while there were still issues with check-in and payment systems, most flights were now running. Hong Kong International Airport has resumed normal operations, according to Chinese state media. Meanwhile, JP Morgan Chase, the biggest bank in the US, said it is working to restore service to ATM machines. The website Downdetector, which detects sites which may be having tech issues, showed fewer sites in the UK which were experiencing problems by the end of the day. CrowdStrike CEO George Kurtz said on X that a defect was found "in a single content update for Windows hosts". "We're deeply sorry for the impact that we've caused to customers, to travellers, to anyone affected by this, including our company," he told the NBC network. "Many of the customers are rebooting the system and it's coming up and it'll be operational. "It could be some time for some systems that just automatically won't recover, but it is our mission... to make sure every customer is fully recovered." Microsoft has also said that several reboots may be required, with some users reporting that as many as 15 could be needed before the problem is fixed. Also, tech experts say CrowdStrike's fix will have to be applied separately to each and every device affected. By 18:00 GMT, aviation data from Cirium suggested that more than 4,000 flights - or 3.9% of the total - had been cancelled so far on Friday, though the figure may also include flights cancelled for other reasons. Payment systems, banking and healthcare providers around the world were affected. It is thought the outage may also have a longer term effect as companies struggle to pay wages to staff, particularly where payments are made on a weekly basis. Some railway companies warned of delays, and broadcasters Sky News and ABC Australia both experienced outages.

extraction.body: From Asia to the U.S., Microsoft’s outage involving services like Outlook and Teams has dragged on for hours and impacted many users, companies and some government operations as the technology giant struggled with fixing the issue. Microsoft said the outage was affecting a wide range of Microsoft 365 offerings that interact with its Exchange Online and email services. Services including Outlook, Teams and AI assistant Copilot were reported by users to be down. The extent of the outage wasn’t clear but the company said in January that it had more than 450 million paid Microsoft 365 commercial subscriptions. The company indicated that its recovery efforts were making progress Friday, saying it was “seeing encouraging recovery progress, with service availability and email delivery performance improving across a growing portion of affected Microsoft 365 infrastructure." Though the company cautioned "some users may still experience intermittent issues as recovery actions continue." But problems appeared to persist, according to an outage tracking site, status reports from organizations that depend on the company's services and anecdotal reports on social media. The Redmond, Washington-based company said it was trying different ways to identify the cause of the problem and get its servers back online, using “a measured approach to identify and repair affected infrastructure.” The company said it did not have any indication that the outage was caused by malicious activity and would treat the incident “with urgency and priority until full resolution.” A series of posts by the company on X suggested its engineers were struggling to get the problem fully under control. Hours after saying it managed to successfully restore service health and functionality, the company said it had updated its list of impacted services and was continuing to address the issue. An earlier post offered little hope for users expecting a quick resolution. “We’ve monitored the status of the changes applied to improve serviceability and confirmed they’re not taking as expected,” the company wrote. In a pair of more recent updates on Friday, Microsoft said “we’re seeing early stabilization and capacity improvements as recovery actions continue.” “Recovery actions are ongoing across affected Microsoft 365 infrastructure and progressing in phases,” the company said in a second post. “We’re seeing incremental improvement in several workloads, but service health remains variable and capacity has not yet fully returned to baseline.” U.S.-based industrial technology company Workhorse Group Inc. delayed a conference call for its quarterly earnings because of the outage. In Australia, Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke said Friday Microsoft had likened the widespread outage to the CrowdStrike outage in 2024. Burke said he had spoken to Microsoft’s top executive in Australia and the government’s national cybersecurity coordinator about the global disruption. "They (Microsoft) don’t believe they are dealing with a cyberattack. They believe that they are dealing in some ways (with something) similar to what we saw with respect to CrowdStrike where there is an update that has gone awry,” Burke told reporters in Sydney. In July 2024, a massive global tech outage grounded flights, disrupted hospitals, banks and retailers, with Texas-based cybersecurity firm CrowdStrike blaming a faulty update to computers running Microsoft Windows that allowed its systems to push bad data out to millions of customer machines. Hong Kong businessperson Danny Lau, who runs an aluminum firm, said his company's Outlook accounts could not receive updates from their U.S. customers due to the outage. If the situation dragged on further, this could “impact the production timeline,” he said. Some banks in Hong Kong, an Asian financial hub, also saw part of their operations disrupted. Air India said its flight operations were unaffected by the global Microsoft outage. However, it temporarily rerouted its email services to ensure customer queries continued to reach the airline without interruption, the company said in a statement. IndiGo, another Indian airline company, said it also reported disruptions to its email support services, which affected its ability to receive customer queries. The airline in a statement on X said its other support channels remained operational and its flight operations were unaffected. Singapore’s Government Technology Agency said that government emails were down and that the agency is working with Microsoft to resolve the issue. The Philippines' Supreme Court said in a statement on X that the ongoing Microsoft 365 service outage has affected some of its operations, including email responses. In Japan , Deputy Chief Cabinet Secretary Masanao Ozaki said the outage impacted the government’s IT infrastructure and that they were “keeping a close eye on the developments.” Japanese authorities had taken steps including securing alternative communication tools such as telephones, the government said. OpenAI and Anthropic each reported that they were facing problems connecting with Microsoft 365 tools, underscoring the ripple effects of outages as more people use artificial intelligence platforms to interact with other companies’ software.

passages: Schools, councils and other organisations across Northern Ireland are among those impacted by a global Microsoft outage.
Microsoft 365 is also used by companies worldwide and is expected to have a knock-on effect to other services.
In a statement Lisburn and Castlereagh City Council said they are aware of the "ongoing global disruption" and will share "further updates if necessary".
Microsoft 365 Services, including Teams, Outlook and Microsoft's artificial intelligence software Copilot, have been affected by "connectivity problems".

Microsoft 365 is also used by companies worldwide and is expected to have a knock-on effect to other services. Microsoft 365 Services, including Teams, Outlook and Microsoft's artificial intelligence software Copilot, have been affected by "connectivity problems".

extraction.body: Schools, councils and other organisations across Northern Ireland are among those impacted by a global Microsoft outage. Problems with the software giant started on Thursday, with monitoring website Downdetector seeing problems reported in more than 70 countries. Microsoft has said it is seeing "encouraging recovery progress" in Europe, and North America is "improving", but adds "some users may still experience intermittent issues". Earlier, it said the issue wasn't caused by a cyber-security breach Public bodies such as the Education Authority said on Friday: "Outlook is currently unavailable to NI schools and the Education Authority. Emails cannot currently be sent or received." The South Eastern Health Trust said there will be "no impact on clinical services". Northern Ireland Ambulance Service said that patient services are not impacted by the outage. Some councils in Northern Ireland have said that their emails systems have been impacted. Belfast City Council said it is experiencing issues "receiving and responding" to emails. "Our website and phone lines are operating as normal however, and customers can still log requests." In a statement Lisburn and Castlereagh City Council said they are aware of the "ongoing global disruption" and will share "further updates if necessary". Causeway Coast and Glens Borough Council confirmed they have been impacted and said the majority of council services are unaffected however there is disruption to staff's ability to send and receive emails. Queen's University Belfast also said they are experiencing email disruption on Friday. "Our students and staff are currently unable to receive or send emails and may experience difficulties accessing. "As always, staff and students should not use personal email accounts to send, receive or store university-related communications or information." The Police Service of Northern Ireland have issued a statement to say its services are unaffected. Microsoft 365 Services, including Teams, Outlook and Microsoft's artificial intelligence software Copilot, have been affected by "connectivity problems". Customers are reporting varying levels of access - many have not been able to send or receive emails, view certain files or details on their calendar apps. Some users have been able to use Teams and are using messaging and online meeting functions without issues. More than 430 million people use Microsoft 365 apps according to Microsoft's website. The full scale of the outage has not been confirmed, but monitoring website Downdetector had 140,000 people from 74 countries report issues with Outlook on Thursday evening. The real figure affected is likely much higher because Downdetector relies primarily on users self-reporting. Microsoft 365 is also used by companies worldwide and is expected to have a knock-on effect to other services.

Tell us: have you been affected by the Microsoft outage? Microsoft struggles to fix huge outage affecting Outlook and Teams Microsoft reports it is seeing some ‘positive results’ in its efforts to get its services back online for millions of customers around the world. Tell us: have you been affected by the Microsoft outage? Microsoft struggles to fix huge outage affecting Outlook and Teams Across Europe, millions of Microsoft customers will have woken up to the news that the company is strugging to get its services back online. The disruption, which began around 6pm GMT on Thursday, has disrupted key Microsoft services such as Outlook , Teams and Copilot . Initially mainly affecting US users, it has gone on to cause disruption across the Asia-Pacific region. Microsoft has suggested the outage may have been caused by issues with the settings applied to servers responsible for keeping Microsoft 365 up and running. It says it doesn’t believe it is suffering a cyber attack. And it became clear that the problem was pretty serious when the company admitted that the fix was “not taking as expected”. The outage hit government agencies in Australia, Japan and the United States, as well as companies including two massive AI companies – OpenAI and Anthropic. In Japan, the economy, trade and industry minister said the disruption had had a “major impact,” on the world’s fourth-biggest economy. Australia’s spy agency and federal police were among the organizations reporting disruption there, with billions of dollars of damage predicted . The latest word from Microsoft is that it is seeing “positive results for server stability” after applying a software patch. But despite that, the company still reports “Service degradation on Microsoft 365 (Business or Enterprise) and Microsoft consumer products”. Simon Azzopardi, CEO of security firm CoreView, says IT teams need to do three things following the Microsoft outage: “Confirm that security and compliance controls such as data loss prevention, sensitivity labelling and Intune compliance policies are working as intended. Suggestions include “ Microsoft 364 ” (although this might be downgraded to “Microsoft 363” if the problems drag into Saturday!), “ Microsoft No-Pilot ”, “ Friday the 13th: Nightmare on One Microsoft Way ”, and “ Microsoft Long Weekend ” (a nod to how today has been a write-off for some companies around the world). More people who’ve been affected by the outage have been getting in touch with The Guardian, including students, teachers and others who work in education. Jenny is a teacher in SEN [special educational needs] school in Norfolk, England and teaches a four day week. Ordinarily Friday is her rest day and in the morning, she says she logs in and gives access to her colleagues to teach lessons she has pre-prepared and also responds to emails. But, the software firm says its recovery efforts are “progressing” ( which seems to be a gentle way of saying the issue isn’t fixed yet! ) This issue affects Outlook.com, OneDrive, OneNote, Microsoft To Do, Teams, and Microsoft 365 for the web. Readers in the US may be surprised to wake up to the news that Microsoft's outage is not fixed! Reminder, it reported around 45 minutes ago that the situation was improving in Europe, Japan and North America . Many Microsoft 365 services are affected, for example: Problems with Exchange Online mean users may be unable to access their mailbox using Outlook on the web Microsoft 365 Education features including Assignments, Reading Progress, and Speaker Progress may be impacted. Microsoft Copilot 365 – users may be unable to load Copilot Chat or receive responses in the web and desktop apps The Microsoft To Do app may not load, and users may see operation failures. Most of the core functionality including joining calls, meetings, group chats, and channel messages are not impacted. Scenarios that depend on Exchange Online, including Calendar related failures with scheduling, invites, viewing, and meeting edits. Creation of Live or Virtual events fail. Failures with Copilot responses for outlook, calendar, or M365 files, read history, or adding to new chats. Navigating to App chats, adding new contacts or syncing contacts in settings fail. Standard channels are working fine but users may experience the inability to create or delete private or shared channels. That suggests there’s progress bringing Outlook back online. Ofqual , the exam regulator for England, is the latest educational institution to be hit by the Microsoft outage. This morning it advised users that its complaints service was not functioning: “We are currently experiencing issues with this service, related to the global Microsoft outage. “We are currently unable to receive complaints, whistleblowing and malpractice submissions.” It said any urgent enquiries should come by telephone.

Microsoft struggles to fix huge outage affecting Outlook and Teams
Across Europe, millions of Microsoft customers will have woken up to the news that the company is strugging to get its services back online.

The disruption, which began around 6pm GMT on Thursday, has disrupted key Microsoft services such as Outlook , Teams and Copilot . Initially mainly affecting US users, it has gone on to cause disruption across the Asia-Pacific region.

Microsoft has suggested the outage may have been caused by issues with the settings applied to servers responsible for keeping Microsoft 365 up and running. It says it doesn’t believe it is suffering a cyber attack.
And it became clear that the problem was pretty serious when the company admitted that the fix was “not taking as expected”.
The outage hit government agencies in Australia, Japan and the United States, as well as companies including two massive AI companies – OpenAI and Anthropic.
In Japan, the economy, trade and industry minister said the disruption had had a “major impact,” on the world’s fourth-biggest economy.
Australia’s spy agency and federal police were among the organizations reporting disruption there, with billions of dollars of damage predicted .
The latest word from Microsoft is that it is seeing “positive results for server stability” after applying a software patch.
But despite that, the company still reports “Service degradation on Microsoft 365 (Business or Enterprise) and Microsoft consumer products”.
Simon Azzopardi, CEO of security firm CoreView, says IT teams need to do three things following the Microsoft outage:
“Confirm that security and compliance controls such as data loss prevention, sensitivity labelling and Intune compliance policies are working as intended.

Suggestions include “ Microsoft 364 ” (although this might be downgraded to “Microsoft 363” if the problems drag into Saturday!), “ Microsoft No-Pilot ”, “ Friday the 13th: Nightmare on One Microsoft Way ”, and “ Microsoft Long Weekend ” (a nod to how today has been a write-off for some companies around the world).
More people who’ve been affected by the outage have been getting in touch with The Guardian, including students, teachers and others who work in education.

Jenny is a teacher in SEN [special educational needs] school in Norfolk, England and teaches a four day week. Ordinarily Friday is her rest day and in the morning, she says she logs in and gives access to her colleagues to teach lessons she has pre-prepared and also responds to emails.
But, the software firm says its recovery efforts are “progressing” ( which seems to be a gentle way of saying the issue isn’t fixed yet! )
This issue affects Outlook.com, OneDrive, OneNote, Microsoft To Do, Teams, and Microsoft 365 for the web.
Readers in the US may be surprised to wake up to the news that Microsoft's outage is not fixed!
Reminder, it reported around 45 minutes ago that the situation was improving in Europe, Japan and North America .
Many Microsoft 365 services are affected, for example:
Problems with Exchange Online mean users may be unable to access their mailbox using Outlook on the web
Microsoft 365 Education features including Assignments, Reading Progress, and Speaker Progress may be impacted.
Microsoft Copilot 365 – users may be unable to load Copilot Chat or receive responses in the web and desktop apps
The Microsoft To Do app may not load, and users may see operation failures.

Most of the core functionality including joining calls, meetings, group chats, and channel messages are not impacted. Scenarios that depend on Exchange Online, including Calendar related failures with scheduling, invites, viewing, and meeting edits. Creation of Live or Virtual events fail. Failures with Copilot responses for outlook, calendar, or M365 files, read history, or adding to new chats.

Navigating to App chats, adding new contacts or syncing contacts in settings fail. Standard channels are working fine but users may experience the inability to create or delete private or shared channels.
That suggests there’s progress bringing Outlook back online.
Ofqual , the exam regulator for England, is the latest educational institution to be hit by the Microsoft outage. This morning it advised users that its complaints service was not functioning:
“We are currently experiencing issues with this service, related to the global Microsoft outage.
“We are currently unable to receive complaints, whistleblowing and malpractice submissions.”
It said any urgent enquiries should come by telephone.

extraction.body: Microsoft suffered a widespread outage on Thursday and Friday, causing disruption to millions of its customers as engineers scrambled to fix one of its biggest-ever server issues. Connectivity problems began shortly before 1 p.m. ET on Thursday and continued into Friday, with Outlook and Teams, along with multiple Microsoft 365 services such as Sharepoint and Copilot, affected. Numerous external services that connect with Microsoft products such as Outlook Calendar were also hit. In an update shortly before 8 a.m. ET, Microsoft continued to warn that users may be unable to connect to multiple Microsoft 365 products, including Outlook on either web or desktop and many services that interact with email. However, it said it was making "continued recovery progress" overall, with "broader improvements" in North America, "sustained improvements" in much of Europe and "encouraging recovery signals" in Asia Pacific. Intermittent issues are expected as recovery efforts continue. Email and related tools were unavailable for Microsoft users on Thursday afternoon and evening, throughout the Asian business day on Friday and across the European and early U.S. morning. Engineering teams have been taking affected systems offline for fixes and bringing them back online in stages. They are prioritizing efforts to preserve emails delayed during the recovery process and reduce email queues and backlogs, extending the timeout window, whereby delayed emails continue to attempt delivery, to 48 hours to help protect messages. Microsoft says it has not detected any malicious activity causing the outage, which it initially blamed on a traffic surge in part of its infrastructure and issues with a component responsible for processing server health. The company said in its initial updates on Thursday that the connectivity problems related to infrastructure "elevated load across multiple regions," caused by a "number of servers being unexpectedly unavailable; straining the remaining infrastructure." Some servers were failing automated health checks, it said. Microsoft shares were around 2% lower in premarket trade. Governments and businesses in Asia-Pacific and Europe said they were monitoring the situation, which was causing widespread disruption. The U.K.'s National Health Service said the outage was affecting some of its services but that patients should attend appointments as normal. Calls "may be subject to long waits" as a result of disruption to the organization, a hospital group serving South West London and the English county of Surrey said on X. Earnings for Swiss luxury goods giant Richemont were slightly delayed on Friday due to the outage. Electric truck maker Workhorse Group, which was expected to report third-quarter results on Nov. 12, rescheduled the release to Nov. 16, citing business disruptions caused by the global Microsoft outage. Air India said it had "temporarily rerouted" emails so it could continue to receive customer messages, adding that its flight operations were not affected. Australian Home Affairs and Cyber Security Minister Tony Burke said in a press conference that Microsoft "believe they are dealing in some ways similar to what we saw with respect to CrowdStrike where there is an update that has gone awry," Reuters reported. A fault with an update issued by cybersecurity company CrowdStrike caused one of the world's biggest IT system outages in 2024 , hitting airlines, banks and more. Microsoft reported in 2025 that Copilot, its collection of AI assistants and tools, had more than 100 million monthly active users. The incident highlights a business "resilience and dependency issue that has been decades in the making," James Owen, managing partner of Digital Risks at consultancy Control Risks, said by phone. "We have become, organizationally in the private sector and more broadly, increasingly dependent on a smaller segment of technology and infrastructure as critical to daily life and business activities." "Organizations are becoming more aware through a geopolitical lens about what technologies they adopt, whether their services are provided by firms in the U.S., or China, or elsewhere, but this shows the importance of proper recovery planning in the case of an IT outage. That could be manual backups, protocols that do not require internet connection, investing in diverse suppliers and crisis management planning rehearsals," he said. Amazon Web Services and Google users also reported outages on the site on Thursday. Amazon wrote on X that services were "operating normally" and an "unrelated disruption elsewhere on the internet is prompting some inaccurate news reports." The company referred users to its health dashboard for "accurate data." At 4 p.m. ET Thursday, Microsoft said it had "validated an alternative service health check method" that brought some affected servers back online. "We're now applying this change more broadly," Microsoft wrote. sources.title: Outlook, Microsoft 365, Teams and more down for millions worldwide — live updates on massive outage
passages: Something is seriously wrong with Microsoft Outlook and other popular Microsoft services like Teams, Microsoft 365, Copilot and others.

While Outlook is getting the most attention in terms of raw reports, it's actually the whole of Microsoft 365 that's having problems, so other services are also experiencing outages that are impacting users, just not at the same scale as Outlook.

The company took to X to update users that it's "working to mitigate impact" and has "confirmed the issue may affect Microsoft 365 service connectivity for users in any region." It didn't provide an updated time for when everything would be back to normal, but hopefully it can get things sorted quickly so emails and calendar alerts can start going again.
Downdetector reports have dropped below 100,000 for Outlook, which likely means that some of Microsoft's traffic-redistribution methods are working for at least some percentage of users.

Microsoft jumped on its 365 Status X account with another update, this time it said, "We've not identified any recent change correlated with the start of impact; however, our investigation indicates the failed health checks may originate from a specific component that's responsible for processing server health.

Microsoft appears to have found the cause, as it posted on X saying that "We've determined a portion of infrastructure is experiencing elevated load across multiple regions, which is likely contributing to the connectivity errors." It quickly followed up with another post saying, "We've begun redistributing connection traffic across our broader worldwide infrastructure to help balance the load." It sounds like the company might have a solution to the problem, though I have to assume that redistributing that much traffic will take some time, so it might be a while before everything is working flawlessly.

As of this post, Microsoft Outlook is sitting at more about 119,000 reports on Downdetector, which is a bit down from the peak of 130,000 but still a staggeringly large number of people having an issue with the productivity service.
We're investigating what's causing these servers to become unavailable while we work to safely return them to service," reads the latest update on Microsoft's status page.

It's still one of the bigger outage numbers we've seen in recent months, so we're by no means out of the woods yet, but between slightly lower reports and Microsoft having a strong idea of what went wrong, we could be in good shape.
So far, 99% of the people who've voted in the poll above are experiencing issues with Outlook.
Microsoft is aware of the issue and working on it.

extraction.body: Something is seriously wrong with Microsoft Outlook and other popular Microsoft services like Teams, Microsoft 365, Copilot and others. More than 100,000 users are flocking to the popular outage-reporting website Downdetector to report issues. Reports began to emerge yesterday at around 12:00 pm ET and although reports have dropped, there are still widespread problems across Microsoft's products. For its part, Microsoft has posted on X to its Microsoft 365 Status account about the issue and what it's doing to get things back in order. I eventually got the Microsoft 365 status page to load, and it's been keeping us updated on the latest issues. As of this post, Microsoft Outlook is sitting at more about 119,000 reports on Downdetector, which is a bit down from the peak of 130,000 but still a staggeringly large number of people having an issue with the productivity service. Microsoft is aware of the issue and working on it. The company took to X to update users that it's "working to mitigate impact" and has "confirmed the issue may affect Microsoft 365 service connectivity for users in any region." It didn't provide an updated time for when everything would be back to normal, but hopefully it can get things sorted quickly so emails and calendar alerts can start going again. While Outlook is getting the most attention in terms of raw reports, it's actually the whole of Microsoft 365 that's having problems, so other services are also experiencing outages that are impacting users, just not at the same scale as Outlook. Microsoft appears to have found the cause, as it posted on X saying that "We've determined a portion of infrastructure is experiencing elevated load across multiple regions, which is likely contributing to the connectivity errors." It quickly followed up with another post saying, "We've begun redistributing connection traffic across our broader worldwide infrastructure to help balance the load." It sounds like the company might have a solution to the problem, though I have to assume that redistributing that much traffic will take some time, so it might be a while before everything is working flawlessly. Downdetector reports have dropped below 100,000 for Outlook, which likely means that some of Microsoft's traffic-redistribution methods are working for at least some percentage of users. While user reports are dropping, I personally still can't access the status page for Microsoft, so I'm forced to turn to X for the latest news (which isn't always as quick as going straight to the source). After about 5 minutes, I went back to the tab and saw that it finally loaded (probably took extra time due to whatever techniques Microsoft is using to re-route traffic). Is this a sign that the outage is almost over? Maybe, but according to the now-loading status page, things are still very much not over. Digging a little deeper into Microsoft's status page, we can see that the company says it has "completed redistributing connection traffic across our worldwide infrastructure, and we're moving additional traffic off the affected infrastructure to further reduce load." That sounds like a big step in the right direction for getting things back in working order. "We're also restarting affected servers to return them to service. We'll see if things start to come back to normal for Outlook and other Microsoft users (officially, Microsoft lists Exchange Online, Microsoft Teams,SharePoint Online, Microsoft Copilot 365 and Microsoft Defender XDR as affected services). That's about 10,000 down from the peak, but still a fairly high number. We're investigating what's causing these servers to become unavailable while we work to safely return them to service," reads the latest update on Microsoft's status page. We're working to safely return them to service," the company posted on X. If Microsoft is able to get these servers up and running soon, we could be seeing this outage come to an end. Of course, it could take some time or end up being something else causing problems. It's still one of the bigger outage numbers we've seen in recent months, so we're by no means out of the woods yet, but between slightly lower reports and Microsoft having a strong idea of what went wrong, we could be in good shape. In parallel, we've initiated a restart of all affected servers and are monitoring health as they return to service," the company posted on X and to its status page. So far, 99% of the people who've voted in the poll above are experiencing issues with Outlook. Given that it has thousands of votes in that direction, I think it's pretty clear we aren't done with this outage yet. However, some users are reporting actual statuses and information if you're willing to dig through all the memes and jokes. Microsoft jumped on its 365 Status X account with another update, this time it said, "We've not identified any recent change correlated with the start of impact; however, our investigation indicates the failed health checks may originate from a specific component that's responsible for processing server health. We've taken steps to prevent additional servers from being impacted while we work to return the affected servers to service." It sounds like it's doing what it can to mitigate the damage caused by the servers being down, but it doesn't have a solution to bring the affected one back online yet. coreStoryFacts.text: Tell us: have you been affected by the Microsoft outage?
This morning it advised users that its complaints service was not functioning:
Microsoft struggles to fix huge outage affecting Outlook and Teams
The disruption, which began around 6pm GMT on Thursday, has disrupted key Microsoft services such as Outlook , Teams and Copilot .
Initially mainly affecting US users, it has gone on to cause disruption across the Asia-Pacific region.

Suggestions include “ Microsoft 364 ” (although this might be downgraded to “Microsoft 363” if the problems drag into Saturday!), “ Microsoft No-Pilot ”, “ Friday the 13th: Nightmare on One Microsoft Way ”, and “ Microsoft Long Weekend ” (a nod to how today has been a write-off for some companies around the world).
“We are currently experiencing issues with this service, related to the global Microsoft outage.
Across Europe, millions of Microsoft customers will have woken up to the news that the company is strugging to get its services back online.
Microsoft has suggested the outage may have been caused by issues with the settings applied to servers responsible for keeping Microsoft 365 up and running.
It says it doesn’t believe it is suffering a cyber attack.
This issue affects Outlook.com, OneDrive, OneNote, Microsoft To Do, Teams, and Microsoft 365 for the web.
The latest word from Microsoft is that it is seeing “positive results for server stability” after applying a software patch.
Microsoft 365 Education features including Assignments, Reading Progress, and Speaker Progress may be impacted.
Many Microsoft 365 services are affected, for example:
Microsoft Copilot 365 – users may be unable to load Copilot Chat or receive responses in the web and desktop apps
ET, Microsoft continued to warn that users may be unable to connect to multiple Microsoft 365 products, including Outlook on either web or desktop and many services that interact with email.
Connectivity problems began shortly before 1 p.m.
Numerous external services that connect with Microsoft products such as Outlook Calendar were also hit.

However, it said it was making "continued recovery progress" overall, with "broader improvements" in North America, "sustained improvements" in much of Europe and "encouraging recovery signals" in Asia Pacific.
Earnings for Swiss luxury goods giant Richemont were slightly delayed on Friday due to the outage.
Electric truck maker Workhorse Group, which was expected to report third-quarter results on Nov.
16, citing business disruptions caused by the global Microsoft outage.
Microsoft reported in 2025 that Copilot, its collection of AI assistants and tools, had more than 100 million monthly active users.
ET Thursday, Microsoft said it had "validated an alternative service health check method" that brought some affected servers back online.

Connectivity problems began shortly before 1 p.m. ET on Thursday and continued into Friday, with Outlook and Teams, along with multiple Microsoft 365 services such as Sharepoint and Copilot, affected. Numerous external services that connect with Microsoft products such as Outlook Calendar were also hit. In an update shortly before 8 a.m. ET, Microsoft continued to warn that users may be unable to connect to multiple Microsoft 365 products, including Outlook on either web or desktop and many services that interact with email. However, it said it was making "continued recovery progress" overall, with "broader improvements" in North America, "sustained improvements" in much of Europe and "encouraging recovery signals" in Asia Pacific. Intermittent issues are expected as recovery efforts continue. Email and related tools were unavailable for Microsoft users on Thursday afternoon and evening, throughout the Asian business day on Friday and across the European and early U.S. morning. Engineering teams have been taking affected systems offline for fixes and bringing them back online in stages. They are prioritizing efforts to preserve emails delayed during the recovery process and reduce email queues and backlogs, extending the timeout window, whereby delayed emails continue to attempt delivery, to 48 hours to help protect messages. Microsoft says it has not detected any malicious activity causing the outage, which it initially blamed on a traffic surge in part of its infrastructure and issues with a component responsible for processing server health. The company said in its initial updates on Thursday that the connectivity problems related to infrastructure "elevated load across multiple regions," caused by a "number of servers being unexpectedly unavailable; straining the remaining infrastructure." Some servers were failing automated health checks, it said. Microsoft shares were around 2% lower in premarket trade. Governments and businesses in Asia-Pacific and Europe said they were monitoring the situation, which was causing widespread disruption. The U.K.'s National Health Service said the outage was affecting some of its services but that patients should attend appointments as normal. Calls "may be subject to long waits" as a result of disruption to the organization, a hospital group serving South West London and the English county of Surrey said on X. Earnings for Swiss luxury goods giant Richemont were slightly delayed on Friday due to the outage. Electric truck maker Workhorse Group, which was expected to report third-quarter results on Nov. 12, rescheduled the release to Nov. 16, citing business disruptions caused by the global Microsoft outage. Air India said it had "temporarily rerouted" emails so it could continue to receive customer messages, adding that its flight operations were not affected. Australian Home Affairs and Cyber Security Minister Tony Burke said in a press conference that Microsoft "believe they are dealing in some ways similar to what we saw with respect to CrowdStrike where there is an update that has gone awry," Reuters reported. A fault with an update issued by cybersecurity company CrowdStrike caused one of the world's biggest IT system outages in 2024 , hitting airlines, banks and more. Microsoft reported in 2025 that Copilot, its collection of AI assistants and tools, had more than 100 million monthly active users. The incident highlights a business "resilience and dependency issue that has been decades in the making," James Owen, managing partner of Digital Risks at consultancy Control Risks, said by phone. "We have become, organizationally in the private sector and more broadly, increasingly dependent on a smaller segment of technology and infrastructure as critical to daily life and business activities." "Organizations are becoming more aware through a geopolitical lens about what technologies they adopt, whether their services are provided by firms in the U.S., or China, or elsewhere, but this shows the importance of proper recovery planning in the case of an IT outage. That could be manual backups, protocols that do not require internet connection, investing in diverse suppliers and crisis management planning rehearsals," he said. Amazon Web Services and Google users also reported outages on the site on Thursday. Amazon wrote on X that services were "operating normally" and an "unrelated disruption elsewhere on the internet is prompting some inaccurate news reports." The company referred users to its health dashboard for "accurate data." At 4 p.m. ET Thursday, Microsoft said it had "validated an alternative service health check method" that brought some affected servers back online. sources.title: Outlook, Microsoft 365, Teams and more down for millions worldwide — live updates on massive outage
passages: Something is seriously wrong with Microsoft Outlook and other popular Microsoft services like Teams, Microsoft 365, Copilot and others.

While Outlook is getting the most attention in terms of raw reports, it's actually the whole of Microsoft 365 that's having problems, so other services are also experiencing outages that are impacting users, just not at the same scale as Outlook.

The company took to X to update users that it's "working to mitigate impact" and has "confirmed the issue may affect Microsoft 365 service connectivity for users in any region." It didn't provide an updated time for when everything would be back to normal, but hopefully it can get things sorted quickly so emails and calendar alerts can start going again.
Downdetector reports have dropped below 100,000 for Outlook, which likely means that some of Microsoft's traffic-redistribution methods are working for at least some percentage of users.

Microsoft jumped on its 365 Status X account with another update, this time it said, "We've not identified any recent change correlated with the start of impact; however, our investigation indicates the failed health checks may originate from a specific component that's responsible for processing server health.

Microsoft appears to have found the cause, as it posted on X saying that "We've determined a portion of infrastructure is experiencing elevated load across multiple regions, which is likely contributing to the connectivity errors." It quickly followed up with another post saying, "We've begun redistributing connection traffic across our broader worldwide infrastructure to help balance the load." It sounds like the company might have a solution to the problem, though I have to assume that redistributing that much traffic will take some time, so it might be a while before everything is working flawlessly.

As of this post, Microsoft Outlook is sitting at more about 119,000 reports on Downdetector, which is a bit down from the peak of 130,000 but still a staggeringly large number of people having an issue with the productivity service.
We're investigating what's causing these servers to become unavailable while we work to safely return them to service," reads the latest update on Microsoft's status page.

It's still one of the bigger outage numbers we've seen in recent months, so we're by no means out of the woods yet, but between slightly lower reports and Microsoft having a strong idea of what went wrong, we could be in good shape.
So far, 99% of the people who've voted in the poll above are experiencing issues with Outlook.
Microsoft is aware of the issue and working on it.

extraction.body: Something is seriously wrong with Microsoft Outlook and other popular Microsoft services like Teams, Microsoft 365, Copilot and others. More than 100,000 users are flocking to the popular outage-reporting website Downdetector to report issues. Reports began to emerge yesterday at around 12:00 pm ET and although reports have dropped, there are still widespread problems across Microsoft's products. For its part, Microsoft has posted on X to its Microsoft 365 Status account about the issue and what it's doing to get things back in order. I eventually got the Microsoft 365 status page to load, and it's been keeping us updated on the latest issues. As of this post, Microsoft Outlook is sitting at more about 119,000 reports on Downdetector, which is a bit down from the peak of 130,000 but still a staggeringly large number of people having an issue with the productivity service. Microsoft is aware of the issue and working on it. The company took to X to update users that it's "working to mitigate impact" and has "confirmed the issue may affect Microsoft 365 service connectivity for users in any region." It didn't provide an updated time for when everything would be back to normal, but hopefully it can get things sorted quickly so emails and calendar alerts can start going again. While Outlook is getting the most attention in terms of raw reports, it's actually the whole of Microsoft 365 that's having problems, so other services are also experiencing outages that are impacting users, just not at the same scale as Outlook. Microsoft appears to have found the cause, as it posted on X saying that "We've determined a portion of infrastructure is experiencing elevated load across multiple regions, which is likely contributing to the connectivity errors." It quickly followed up with another post saying, "We've begun redistributing connection traffic across our broader worldwide infrastructure to help balance the load." It sounds like the company might have a solution to the problem, though I have to assume that redistributing that much traffic will take some time, so it might be a while before everything is working flawlessly. Downdetector reports have dropped below 100,000 for Outlook, which likely means that some of Microsoft's traffic-redistribution methods are working for at least some percentage of users. While user reports are dropping, I personally still can't access the status page for Microsoft, so I'm forced to turn to X for the latest news (which isn't always as quick as going straight to the source). After about 5 minutes, I went back to the tab and saw that it finally loaded (probably took extra time due to whatever techniques Microsoft is using to re-route traffic). Is this a sign that the outage is almost over? Maybe, but according to the now-loading status page, things are still very much not over. Digging a little deeper into Microsoft's status page, we can see that the company says it has "completed redistributing connection traffic across our worldwide infrastructure, and we're moving additional traffic off the affected infrastructure to further reduce load." That sounds like a big step in the right direction for getting things back in working order. "We're also restarting affected servers to return them to service. We'll see if things start to come back to normal for Outlook and other Microsoft users (officially, Microsoft lists Exchange Online, Microsoft Teams,SharePoint Online, Microsoft Copilot 365 and Microsoft Defender XDR as affected services). That's about 10,000 down from the peak, but still a fairly high number. We're investigating what's causing these servers to become unavailable while we work to safely return them to service," reads the latest update on Microsoft's status page. We're working to safely return them to service," the company posted on X. If Microsoft is able to get these servers up and running soon, we could be seeing this outage come to an end. Of course, it could take some time or end up being something else causing problems. It's still one of the bigger outage numbers we've seen in recent months, so we're by no means out of the woods yet, but between slightly lower reports and Microsoft having a strong idea of what went wrong, we could be in good shape. In parallel, we've initiated a restart of all affected servers and are monitoring health as they return to service," the company posted on X and to its status page. So far, 99% of the people who've voted in the poll above are experiencing issues with Outlook. Given that it has thousands of votes in that direction, I think it's pretty clear we aren't done with this outage yet. However, some users are reporting actual statuses and information if you're willing to dig through all the memes and jokes. Microsoft jumped on its 365 Status X account with another update, this time it said, "We've not identified any recent change correlated with the start of impact; however, our investigation indicates the failed health checks may originate from a specific component that's responsible for processing server health. We've taken steps to prevent additional servers from being impacted while we work to return the affected servers to service." It sounds like it's doing what it can to mitigate the damage caused by the servers being down, but it doesn't have a solution to bring the affected one back online yet. As usual, Reddit users have some funny takes on the outage. Not many of them are particularly helpful, but if you're looking for some entertainment while you can't get things done, it might be worth checking out this thread and having a laugh. Of course, if you have your own witty comments, you're welcome to scroll down this page and leave a comment here; we read them all! "While we haven't identified any recent changes that correlate with the start of impact, our investigation indicates the failed health checks may originate from a specific component on the affected servers that's responsible for processing them. We're deploying a targeted change to bypass this component on a subset of servers to validate whether this restores availability, and we've taken steps to prevent additional servers from being removed from service while we work to return the affected servers to service. Usually, when something is fixed during an outage, we see a sharp drop in the number of reports; a gradual decline likely indicates that people just aren't reporting as much as when the outage first started.

Open-weight artificial intelligence could lose one of its most influential supporters following the board-led ouster of Nvidia co-founder Jensen Huang, potentially changing the direction of an industry in which the chipmaker has championed alternatives to closed AI systems. The push for openly available AI model weights is one of several efforts Huang helped organize that could suffer after his resignation following his admission of an extramarital affair, TechCrunch argued . Nvidia makes open-weight models available alongside open-source tools for AI agents and security. These models give businesses more choices and can help reduce costs. In July, Huang coordinated a letter in favor of open-weight models that attracted hundreds of signatures. The effort followed reported lobbying by Anthropic and OpenAI for restrictions on Chinese open-weight models. TechCrunch identified Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella as another prominent supporter, though the outlet observed that Nadella hasn't organized the industry around the issue as visibly as Huang. Beyond supporting open-weight models, Huang helped finance the infrastructure needed to power AI. According to Bloomberg reporting cited in the analysis, Nvidia had committed to $750 billion in deals by July in which its investments helped companies expand and purchase its chips. That expansion has consequences for the energy grid: Data centers need electricity to run processors and cooling equipment. While AI can help optimize clean energy systems, the infrastructure behind it also consumes substantial amounts of electricity and water. Forbes reported that nearly half of the year's approximately $80 billion in data center bond offerings carried high-risk "junk" ratings, TechCrunch noted. Nvidia also agreed in August to guarantee $105 billion in funding for an OpenAI facility in Ohio, CNBC reported . Alongside its infrastructure investments, Nvidia has pursued technical approaches to AI safety. Its Open Agent Safety Platform attracted more than 100 participating companies, creating a largely open-source effort to address misbehaving AI agents. The initiative followed incidents involving OpenAI and Anthropic agents accessing others' networks or engaging in other misconduct. Huang advocated industry-led safety measures. TechCrunch posited that his departure weakens that approach by removing its most visible champion. Another initiative looks to move some AI work onto personal computers. Huang recruited PC manufacturers to develop high-end systems designed to run agents locally, targeting creators, developers, and other users already familiar with the technology. Those machines are scheduled to debut for the 2026 holiday shopping season. Nvidia's planned $12.9 billion acquisition of Hugging Face, a major hosting platform for open-weight models, is scheduled to close in the first half of 2027, subject to regulatory approval. Huang's push for open-weight AI touches on questions about safety, energy use, and access to computing hardware. • Trump called AI danger talk a "hoax" during a phone call to Huang. • Huang said AI must cause "pain and suffering" before helping the climate. • Anthropic's Dario Amodei urged an AI slowdown and outside access to check model safety practices. • OpenAI's Sam Altman said the upsides justify some AI misuse , diverging from Anthropic. sources.title: Jensen Huang's exit from Nvidia raises critical questions about the future of AI - CNBC
passages: Michael Dell described Jensen Huang as a "visionary of the AI age." Deutsche Telekom CEO Tim Höttges said a photo with the Nvidia CEO produced more media coverage for his company than its iPhone launch.
During the keynote of his annual Dreamforce conference, Salesforce's Marc Benioff said, "Jensen, we're all following you, bro," as the two paced through the audience.
Executives at numerous Nvidia customers, partners and portfolio companies told CNBC that Huang frequently emailed or called CEOs to offer his help in challenging times.
When it comes to investing cash in fledgling startups, Huang is known to host entrepreneurs at Nvidia's Silicon Valley headquarters.

While there could be 30 Nvidia employees in the room for the pitch meeting, only Huang asks questions, according to people with knowledge of the matter, who requested anonymity because they're not authorized to speak publicly about it.
That approach persisted, as recently as this week.
Fireworks, which Nvidia first backed in 2024, was dealing with a series of high-profile cyberattacks.
It had been a tumultuous stretch for Nvidia, even before the Huang saga led the board to launch an investigation of the CEO's behavior and the potential national security implications.
The stock is on pace for its sixth straight weekly drop, which would be the longest losing streak since 2012.

That includes a 9% slump last week after the midterm elections resulted in sweeping Democratic victories in both chambers of Congress, and the passage of dozens of ballot measures that could slow the buildout of new data centers.
In May, Huang joined President Donald Trump on Air Force One for a trip to China to meet with President Xi Jinping .

Three months later, Huang gathered six of the biggest names at the Nasdaq to announce on CNBC a proposed $500 billion artificial intelligence buildout plan, cementing his central role at the intersection of Wall Street and Silicon Valley.
"How companies handle a crisis determines their future," former Cisco CEO John Chambers, now a startup investor, told CNBC's " Fast Money " on Wednesday.
"How they handle this will determine if they're a great company and a great leadership team beyond one person."
Huang's ambitions extended well beyond the U.S.

He wanted to be a force in China, which became a difficult market for Nvidia during the Biden administration and was virtually off-limits after Trump implemented strict export controls in his second term.
Huang's aggressive pursuit of China may have been his undoing.
"What bothers me at the end of it is what we don't know is what she knows about him that can be utilized," Cramer told CNBC, right before Huang resigned and referring to the affair.
"This is a guy that's right now so vulnerable to extortion, blackmail.
I just don't think, as a national security matter, we can run the risk."
Nvidia is scheduled to report quarterly results on Tuesday, and expectations remain high, with analysts projecting 92% year-over-year revenue growth to $109.2 billion, according to LSEG.
That's up 18-fold from the same quarter in 2022, just before OpenAI launched ChatGPT and kicked off the generative AI era.
Huang wanted the world standardizing on Nvidia.

She has business ties to Megaspeed International, a Singapore-based cloud computing firm and an Nvidia customer that's facing scrutiny over suspicions that it facilitated billions of dollars of restricted Nvidia chips to China.

Tomás Puig, founder and CEO of enterprise AI startup Alembic, said that following the collapse of Silicon Valley Bank in 2023, his company was "down to weeks of cash and Nvidia was our biggest customer."
"I emailed Jensen, and they prepaid two years of invoices so we could keep the lights on and people kept their jobs," Puig told CNBC.
Huang founded Nvidia to make chips for computer graphics, both for video games and rendering.
In the early 2000s, he and other executives saw an opportunity to put GPUs to work for computationally intense projects.
That technology eventually turned Nvidia into the most important player in AI and a key American asset for national defense.
Nvidia has not responded to multiple requests for comment.
On the deal-making side, Huang's top lieutenants were Kress and Vishal Bhagwati, head of corporate development, sources said, though they add that all the big decisions were made by the CEO.
— CNBC's Lora Kolodny, Jordan Novet and Seema Mody contributed to this report.

extraction.body: The open source community just lost one of its strongest advocates. Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang resigned Thursday after he admitted to an affair with an alleged Chinese spy, raising concerns about U.S. national security and the motives behind the executive’s support for softer chip export controls on China. Huang has been a staunch supporter of open source AI, framing the ecosystem as good for safety, innovation, diffusion, and sovereignty. And as frontier AI labs increasingly move to reduce their reliance on Nvidia and build their own chips, supporting open source is also a good way for the company to diversify its customer base by selling chips to nation-states, enterprises, and any organization that wants to own its own models. Still, Huang’s resignation raises questions about whether Nvidia will carry on his legacy by continuing to support the open model community. Jensen no longer being CEO would be very very bad for the open model cause in the US. Huang’s departure also comes as Nvidia has yet to finalize a deal to acquire open source platform Hugging Face for $13 billion . Hugging Face CEO Clem Delangue said in a post on X that the company would continue to fight for open source , whatever happens next. Nvidia also agreed to pay $6 billion for a non-exclusive license for open AI coding startup Poolside’s technology. Within Nvidia, Huang pushed for the development of the Nemotron family of open-weight AI models built for long-running agentic AI systems and reasoning workloads — potential competitors to closed frontier models. One company insider told TechCrunch that they don’t expect a change in leadership to have an impact on Nemotron development. Huang also backed companies that would make American open models more competitive, investing in startups like Reflection AI and Thinking Machines Lab. Huang’s influence extended beyond Nvidia’s investments and product roadmap. He also emerged as one of the most prominent voices pushing back against Washington’s efforts to restrict the open AI ecosystem. Earlier this year, Huang wrote an open letter signed by 25 companies, including Microsoft, Meta, IBM, and Palantir, urging the U.S. government not to over-restrict open-weight AI models, many of which come from China. The impetus for that letter was Washington’s debate over how the U.S. should respond to allegations that Chinese AI labs are stealing intellectual property from American counterparts like Anthropic and OpenAI, both of which have reportedly appealed directly to Washington on the matter, urging stronger protections. That combination of Huang’s personal visibility and Nvidia’s market power made him the strongest counterweight to arguments from closed-model providers like Anthropic and OpenAI, which have advocated for greater restrictions on advanced AI models due to safety reasons. Without Huang, the concern among open source community members is that whoever takes over will be more cautious. Nvidia has named CFO Colette Kress as interim CEO. It’s not clear how Kress will approach the Hugging Face deal or support for the open model ecosystem, but founder-driven priorities tend to get a downgrade when leadership changes. Huang’s exit could also strengthen the arguments of those in Washington who are arguing for tougher restrictions on Chinese AI companies, particularly as the scandal surrounding his relationship with Alice Huang, the Megaspeed executive and alleged spy, puts renewed scrutiny on his efforts to loosen chip export controls. Restrictions on open-weight models from China could kneecap competition for American companies, the most powerful of which have kept their models closed. Still, supporting open source isn’t simply a passion project Huang pursued out of idealism. It’s increasingly central to Nvidia’s business strategy. As some of Nvidia’s biggest customers, including Google and OpenAI, develop their own chips, Nvidia has an incentive to cultivate a much broader ecosystem of AI developers and customers. More players training, fine-tuning, and running models mean more GPUs sold, and less dependence on a handful of frontier labs. Huang may be gone, but Nvidia still needs an open AI ecosystem. The question now is whether that commitment can survive without the man who made it a priority. TechCrunch has reached out to Nvidia for comment. Huang also backed companies that would make American open models more competitive, investing in startups like Reflection AI and Thinking Machines Lab.

Huang’s influence extended beyond Nvidia’s investments and product roadmap. He also emerged as one of the most prominent voices pushing back against Washington’s efforts to restrict the open AI ecosystem.

Earlier this year, Huang wrote an open letter signed by 25 companies, including Microsoft, Meta, IBM, and Palantir, urging the U.S. government not to over-restrict open-weight AI models, many of which come from China.

The impetus for that letter was Washington’s debate over how the U.S. should respond to allegations that Chinese AI labs are stealing intellectual property from American counterparts like Anthropic and OpenAI, both of which have reportedly appealed directly to Washington on the matter, urging stronger protections.

That combination of Huang’s personal visibility and Nvidia’s market power made him the strongest counterweight to arguments from closed-model providers like Anthropic and OpenAI, which have advocated for greater restrictions on advanced AI models due to safety reasons.

Without Huang, the concern among open source community members is that whoever takes over will be more cautious. Nvidia has named CFO Colette Kress as interim CEO. It’s not clear how Kress will approach the Hugging Face deal or support for the open model ecosystem, but founder-driven priorities tend to get a downgrade when leadership changes.

Huang’s exit could also strengthen the arguments of those in Washington who are arguing for tougher restrictions on Chinese AI companies, particularly as the scandal surrounding his relationship with Alice Huang, the Megaspeed executive and alleged spy, puts renewed scrutiny on his efforts to loosen chip export controls.
Restrictions on open-weight models from China could kneecap competition for American companies, the most powerful of which have kept their models closed.
Still, supporting open source isn’t simply a passion project Huang pursued out of idealism. It’s increasingly central to Nvidia’s business strategy.
As some of Nvidia’s biggest customers, including Google and OpenAI, develop their own chips, Nvidia has an incentive to cultivate a much broader ecosystem of AI developers and customers.
More players training, fine-tuning, and running models mean more GPUs sold, and less dependence on a handful of frontier labs.
Huang may be gone, but Nvidia still needs an open AI ecosystem. The question now is whether that commitment can survive without the man who made it a priority.
