Bitcoin (BTC) dropped below $69,000 late Thursday for the first time since August as multiple headwinds, including inflation concerns, rising interest rates, and the ongoing challenges around Nvidia Corp. (NVDA), weighed on the asset. BTC prices slumped nearly 7% over the past day, falling to $68,529.96 at the time of writing. Meanwhile, Ethereum (ETH) prices slipped to $1,912.54. See what 10M+ investors are talking about. Get the Stocktwits Daily Rip for what retail is watching right now, free to your inbox According to market commentator The Kobeissi Letter, the selling pressure led to a loss of about $150 billion in crypto markets over 48 hours. Although Bitcoin is falling to its lowest level in months, some experts believe that now is a good time to enter. Crypto analyst Michaël van de Poppe said in a post on X that he has been buying BTC, outlining five reasons for his move. He noted that the "terrible sentiment" around the underlying asset means it is hard for prices to keep declining, adding that while there have been multiple events for the asset price to crash, it hasn't yet and markets are simply witnessing a 20% correction. He also pointed out that this is a support area, "just barely beneath the 200-Day MA and ideal for liquidity." The analyst said that Bitcoin had already bottomed on the Friday prior to the SpaceX IPO and that he "wouldn't be surprised" if the present scenario was at the same cadence. "Fifthly: Nasdaq is already up a lot, meaning that there's a gap between Bitcoin and the Nasdaq. It doesn't take long for this gap to close, which is why I've been buying Bitcoin today," he said. Meanwhile, Anthony Pompliano, Founder and CEO of Professional Capital Management, said in a post on X, "Bitcoin is falling to prices we haven't seen since…..3 months ago. Everyone relax, so you can realize that AI and bitcoin are one big trade now." However, long-time crypto critic Peter Schiff is not convinced. In a post on X, he implored investors to think about how Bitcoin has been trading relative to 2021. "Think about this, HOLDers. Bitcoin just traded at a lower price than it traded in November 2021. How many of you who owned Bitcoin back then expected it to be below the Nov. 2021 high more than five years later? Bitcoin is in a long-term bear market. The long-term trend is down," he argued. Rich Rosenblum, co-founder of crypto market maker GSR, told Bloomberg that the volatility in the AI trade and continued U.S. dollar strength have impacted some long Bitcoin positions negatively, while the red-hot inflation data and changes in Nvidia Corp.'s (NVDA) leadership amid Jensen Huang's resignation are also weighing on risk assets. Dean Chen, an analyst at crypto exchange Bitunix, also said in a note Thursday, as per Bloomberg, "Bitcoin is showing signs of a changing market structure, with selling pressure concentrated in derivatives while spot market activity remains comparatively resilient." Meanwhile, futures cumulative volume delta, a measure that tracks how aggressive buyers or sellers are in the futures market, has turned deeply negative, he noted, while adding that open interest has also declined. "Taken together, these indicators suggest that leveraged exposure is cooling, but market positioning remains mixed," Chen reportedly said. Crypto-linked equities fell alongside cryptocurrencies late Thursday. Strategy (MSTR), Bitmine Immersion Technologies (BMNR), Strive (ASST), Coinbase Global Inc. (COIN), and Robinhood Markets Inc. (HOOD) all saw their shares decline in the overnight trade. Strategy also faces pressure after MSCI Inc. said it would remove the company from its global indexes after the Nov. 30 rebalancing, likely prompting an exodus from passive funds. Caroline Mauron, co-founder of Orbit Markets, told Bloomberg that MSCI's decision to drop Strategy, which is the largest corporate buyer of BTC, from its global equity benchmarks has also been a factor affecting the cryptocurrency. On Stocktwits, retail sentiment around BTC was 'extremely bearish' at the time of writing, while it was 'bearish' for ETH. Sentiment around MSTR was 'extremely bearish,' while ASST, COIN, and HOOD were in 'bearish' territory. Retail sentiment around BMNR improved from 'neutral' to 'bullish' over 24 hours. BTC has lost nearly 33% of its value in the last one year, while ETH has lost more than 45% in the same time. For updates and corrections, email newsroom[at]stocktwits[dot]com. Aashika Suresh has no position in any of the stocks mentioned in this article. StockTwits' news team content is for informational purposes only and is not intended as investment advice. For more, see our editorial policy . This article was originally published on StockTwits .

Dean Chen, an analyst at crypto exchange Bitunix, also said in a note Thursday, as per Bloomberg, "Bitcoin is showing signs of a changing market structure, with selling pressure concentrated in derivatives while spot market activity remains comparatively resilient."

Meanwhile, futures cumulative volume delta, a measure that tracks how aggressive buyers or sellers are in the futures market, has turned deeply negative, he noted, while adding that open interest has also declined. "Taken together, these indicators suggest that leveraged exposure is cooling, but market positioning remains mixed," Chen reportedly said.

Crypto-linked equities fell alongside cryptocurrencies late Thursday. Strategy (MSTR), Bitmine Immersion Technologies (BMNR), Strive (ASST), Coinbase Global Inc. (COIN), and Robinhood Markets Inc. (HOOD) all saw their shares decline in the overnight trade.
Strategy also faces pressure after MSCI Inc. said it would remove the company from its global indexes after the Nov. 30 rebalancing, likely prompting an exodus from passive funds.

Caroline Mauron, co-founder of Orbit Markets, told Bloomberg that MSCI's decision to drop Strategy, which is the largest corporate buyer of BTC, from its global equity benchmarks has also been a factor affecting the cryptocurrency.

Sentiment around MSTR was 'extremely bearish,' while ASST, COIN, and HOOD were in 'bearish' territory. Retail sentiment around BMNR improved from 'neutral' to 'bullish' over 24 hours.
BTC has lost nearly 33% of its value in the last one year, while ETH has lost more than 45% in the same time.

The latest decline follows the release of hotter-than-expected US Consumer Price Index (CPI) data, raising concerns that the Federal Reserve could maintain a restrictive monetary policy stance for longer. Technical indicators suggest that any recovery attempts could encounter resistance unless broader market sentiment improves. The latest US CPI report has added pressure to an already fragile cryptocurrency market, reinforcing concerns about the Federal Reserve's interest rate outlook. Higher-than-expected inflation generally reduces the likelihood of monetary easing and can strengthen expectations that the central bank will maintain or increase borrowing costs. For Bitcoin, such an environment can be challenging because higher interest rates tend to make traditional yield-bearing assets more attractive relative to speculative investments. Investors are now reassessing the possibility of additional monetary tightening, while traders remain cautious about increasing exposure to risk-sensitive assets. Unless inflation concerns ease or buying demand strengthens, cryptocurrencies could remain vulnerable to additional losses in the coming sessions. passages: United Airlines has prohibited third-party artificial intelligence agents from executing flight reservations on behalf of customers, a move the carrier attributes to security vulnerabilities and potential non-compliance with federal regulations.

The airline is updating its booking and ticketing policies to restrict access for unauthorized, third-party personal AI assistants, effectively blocking these automated tools from interacting directly with its digital platforms or through travel aggregators.

The airline noted that using AI agents to perform routine tasks, such as checking in for a flight, may violate regulations requiring travelers to verify in person that their luggage does not contain prohibited substances.
He noted that flight search processes incur costs for airlines, and United likely seeks to avoid the expense associated with a potential surge in AI bot-generated search queries.

Harteveldt emphasized that while this restriction may limit the ease with which AI tools can navigate fare options, it does not remove United's fares from major aggregators like Kayak, Hopper, and Google Flights.
Consumers can still book United flights through these established platforms, but the direct automation of the purchase process by personal AI agents is now contractually restricted.

extraction.body: United Airlines has prohibited third-party artificial intelligence agents from executing flight reservations on behalf of customers, a move the carrier attributes to security vulnerabilities and potential non-compliance with federal regulations. The airline is updating its booking and ticketing policies to restrict access for unauthorized, third-party personal AI assistants, effectively blocking these automated tools from interacting directly with its digital platforms or through travel aggregators. The ban addresses a specific financial and operational risk: the requirement for AI agents to access sensitive consumer data, including payment credentials and frequent flyer account information. United stated that sharing account credentials with third-party AI assistants exposes users to the risk of unintended purchases, unauthorized account changes, and the misuse of MileagePlus miles. The carrier argues that these automated actions lack the human verification necessary to ensure financial accuracy and account security. Beyond financial security, United cited federal rules as a driver for the restriction. The airline noted that using AI agents to perform routine tasks, such as checking in for a flight, may violate regulations requiring travelers to verify in person that their luggage does not contain prohibited substances. By blocking these automated interactions, United aims to ensure that all booking and compliance steps are completed by verified human users rather than software intermediaries that cannot perform physical inspections. Henry Harteveldt, an aviation analyst at Atmosphere Research Group, interpreted the move as a defensive strategy against additional intermediaries. He noted that flight search processes incur costs for airlines, and United likely seeks to avoid the expense associated with a potential surge in AI bot-generated search queries. Harteveldt emphasized that while this restriction may limit the ease with which AI tools can navigate fare options, it does not remove United's fares from major aggregators like Kayak, Hopper, and Google Flights. Consumers can still book United flights through these established platforms, but the direct automation of the purchase process by personal AI agents is now contractually restricted. This policy stands in contrast to the approach taken by other carriers. Southwest Airlines, for instance, has made its flight inventory accessible to users of ChatGPT, allowing the AI assistant to query and display fare information. United's decision creates a fragmented landscape where the ability of AI agents to book flights depends entirely on individual airline policies, leaving consumers with varying levels of automation support depending on the carrier they choose.

passages: The idea of letting an AI assistant handle everything from finding flights to completing the booking has been gaining traction with AI developers and consumers alike, but not every business in the travel industry is on board with it.One of the biggest names in American aviation, United Airlines, has just drawn a firm line.United Airlines to Block AI Agents From Booking FlightsUnited Airlines has announced it is updating its ticketing policies to restrict AI agents from booking flights through its website, third-party travel agencies, and flight aggregators.

Businesses like United, JPMorgan Chase, and Amazon have moved to block agents over concerns ranging from security and fraud to regulatory compliance and the loss of direct customer relationships.At the same time, other companies including Southwest Airlines are actively building integrations that invite agents into their booking flows.The adoption rate among consumers is still modest: Uber reported that during the week of Halloween 2026, its 320 million trips and deliveries included only 500 AI-agent-driven Uber Eats orders and four rides, suggesting that agentic commerce remains a niche use case despite significant industry attention.

"To be honest, I do not want to create another middleman," Kirby said, articulating a concern that AI agents sitting between United and its customers could erode the direct relationship the airline has built through its own app, website, and loyalty program.Transportation Department, FAA Also Against AI AgentsBeyond United's own business concerns, the airline specifically cited existing federal regulations from the Department of Transportation and the Federal Aviation Administration as reasons why AI agent bookings raise compliance problems that go beyond corporate preference, said Engadget.The FAA and DOT have regulations governing the interaction between airlines and passengers during the booking and check-in process, some of which explicitly require a human acknowledgment or disclosure.

Southwest Airlines took the opposite approach on October 6 when it announced the launch of a first-of-its-kind US airline plugin in ChatGPT, allowing travelers to discover and shop for Southwest flights directly through the AI assistant.Southwest described the plugin as the first step in a phased AI-powered booking approach developed in partnership with OpenAI and Amazon Web Services.

For businesses receiving agent-driven traffic, the concerns center on security, liability, and the dilution of direct consumer relationships.How Do AI Agents Affect the Industry?The question of how AI agents interact with commerce and service businesses is unresolved and playing out in real time across multiple industries simultaneously.

The experience is designed to let travelers move from inspiration and discovery into booking options with Southwest from within a ChatGPT conversation, reducing the number of steps between deciding to travel and completing a purchase."Customers are evolving how they plan their travel, and Southwest is helping to shape what comes next," said Sabrina Callahan, Chief Digital and Marketing Officer at Southwest Airlines.

The plugin is built to allow Southwest to appear earlier in the customer journey and offer a more direct path from intent to booking, with the airline viewing the AI-assisted channel as a way to reach customers where they are already searching.The difference in approach between United and Southwest illustrates that there is no industry-wide consensus on how to handle agentic commerce in travel.

United operates a hub-and-spoke network with hubs at major airports including Chicago O'Hare, Newark Liberty, Houston George Bush Intercontinental, Denver International, Los Angeles International, San Francisco International, and Washington Dulles.The airline is a founding member of the Star Alliance, the world's largest global airline alliance.

The airline joins a growing list of companies, including JPMorgan Chase and Amazon, that have moved to block AI agents from their platforms over security and privacy concerns.United laid out several specific reasons for the restriction. When a customer hands an AI agent access to their account to complete a booking, that agent can potentially expose payment information, login credentials, and loyalty account details, leading to what the airline described as unintended purchases, account changes, or unauthorized use of MileagePlus miles.The company also pointed to a risk unique to air travel: passengers must personally acknowledge that their baggage does not contain hazardous materials during check-in, a legal obligation that only a human being can satisfy.United CEO Scott Kirby was direct about the company's reluctance to embrace agentic commerce during a public appearance this week. An AI agent completing check-in on a customer's behalf cannot satisfy that legal requirement.United's concern about AI agents potentially running afoul of these regulations reflects a broader regulatory uncertainty around agentic AI in contexts where consumer protection and safety rules assume a human is making the transaction. As AI agents become more capable, the question of whether a purchase or acknowledgment made autonomously by an AI on a consumer's behalf meets the same legal standard as one made by the consumer directly is likely to become an active question for regulators across the travel industry and beyond.Some Airlines Still Allow AI Agent Flight BookingNot every airline is responding to the AI agent question the same way United is. Scott Kirby serves as CEO.What Are AI Agents?AI agents are software systems powered by artificial intelligence that are designed to perform tasks autonomously on a user's behalf, often across multiple digital platforms and services. Unlike a standard AI chatbot that answers questions and waits for the next prompt, an AI agent can take actions in the world: logging into accounts, searching for products, filling out forms, completing purchases, sending messages, and managing files, often with little or no additional input after the initial instruction.Examples include Meta's Muse, OpenAI's ChatGPT Dots, and Anthropic's Claude-based agentic workflows, all of which have been built to handle multi-step tasks across connected apps and services. extraction.body: United Airlines has prohibited third-party artificial intelligence agents from executing flight reservations on behalf of customers, a move the carrier attributes to security vulnerabilities and potential non-compliance with federal regulations. The airline is updating its booking and ticketing policies to restrict access for unauthorized, third-party personal AI assistants, effectively blocking these automated tools from interacting directly with its digital platforms or through travel aggregators. The ban addresses a specific financial and operational risk: the requirement for AI agents to access sensitive consumer data, including payment credentials and frequent flyer account information. United stated that sharing account credentials with third-party AI assistants exposes users to the risk of unintended purchases, unauthorized account changes, and the misuse of MileagePlus miles. The carrier argues that these automated actions lack the human verification necessary to ensure financial accuracy and account security. Beyond financial security, United cited federal rules as a driver for the restriction. The airline noted that using AI agents to perform routine tasks, such as checking in for a flight, may violate regulations requiring travelers to verify in person that their luggage does not contain prohibited substances. By blocking these automated interactions, United aims to ensure that all booking and compliance steps are completed by verified human users rather than software intermediaries that cannot perform physical inspections. Henry Harteveldt, an aviation analyst at Atmosphere Research Group, interpreted the move as a defensive strategy against additional intermediaries. He noted that flight search processes incur costs for airlines, and United likely seeks to avoid the expense associated with a potential surge in AI bot-generated search queries. Harteveldt emphasized that while this restriction may limit the ease with which AI tools can navigate fare options, it does not remove United's fares from major aggregators like Kayak, Hopper, and Google Flights. Consumers can still book United flights through these established platforms, but the direct automation of the purchase process by personal AI agents is now contractually restricted. This policy stands in contrast to the approach taken by other carriers. Southwest Airlines, for instance, has made its flight inventory accessible to users of ChatGPT, allowing the AI assistant to query and display fare information. United's decision creates a fragmented landscape where the ability of AI agents to book flights depends entirely on individual airline policies, leaving consumers with varying levels of automation support depending on the carrier they choose.

passages: Companies linked to alleged Chinese spy Alice Huang have invested in Chinese artificial intelligence firm DeepSeek and committed to supplying Nvidia's Blackwell chips, according to a report by The Information.Blackwell is Nvidia's latest generation of graphics processing units (GPUs) and AI accelerators.

Built on the company's Blackwell GPU microarchitecture, it succeeds the older Hopper architecture and is designed to power large-scale artificial intelligence, heavy-duty data centres and high-performance computing.Alice, also known as Alice Wang or Huang Le, is a Chinese businesswoman whose links with Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang and Singapore-based data centre company Megaspeed have come under scrutiny.Meanwhile, Singapore authorities have issued Alice a stern warning and barred her from re-entering the country after finding that she provided inaccurate information during investigations into Megaspeed.Singapore's Ministry of Home Affairs (MHA) said the Singapore Police Force (SPF) assessed that Alice had attempted to mislead investigators to downplay her role in the company.The probe centres on suspected false declarations involving the purchase of servers and other related offences.

According to reports, she was introduced to Jensen through her husband, corporate investor Kang Weigh, around a decade before reports of her alleged relationship with the billionaire executive emerged.Kang had business dealings with Jensen in the 2010s while acquiring Chinese video game companies, a source familiar with the couple told The Information.Chinese media reports suggest that Kang and Alice used their association with Jensen to secure business opportunities over the years.

passages: An investigation reveals a $14 million investment connected to Huang’s business network as questions intensify over Nvidia chip exports, Chinese AI development and the resignation of former CEO Jensen Huang.

According to a November 12, 2026, investigation by The Information, Century Litong and its parent company, Shanghai-listed Jiangsu Lettall Electronics, participated in DeepSeek’s second fundraising round between July and October.
The investment was reportedly intended to strengthen commercial relationships with DeepSeek and establish access to Nvidia’s Blackwell artificial intelligence processors.
One investment vehicle was managed by Monolith Management, which became DeepSeek’s third-largest investor following the financing.
Century Litong, a Chinese cloud computing company established in 2023, reportedly obtained preferred cloud partner status with Nvidia shortly after its founding.
The Information reported that Litong-related companies had imported approximately 240,000 Nvidia processors worth at least $7.5 billion into China since 2023.
The network also reportedly obtained Blackwell processors despite U.S. restrictions on exporting advanced AI chips to China.
However, the investigation did not establish whether the processors allegedly promised to DeepSeek were ultimately delivered.
Her connections were traced through corporate transactions and family relationships.
The fundraising attracted nearly 30 investors, including Tencent and battery manufacturer CATL.
The investments were structured through special-purpose vehicles, meaning the participating companies did not appear directly on DeepSeek’s shareholder register.
Alice Huang previously held an executive position at Singapore-based Megaspeed International, a company involved in providing Nvidia-powered computing infrastructure.
Earlier investigations raised questions about whether commercial arrangements involving Megaspeed and related companies facilitated access to restricted processors.
Huang has also been accused of having connections to Chinese intelligence, but those allegations remain unproven.
Attorney General Todd Blanche confirmed on November 12 that the Justice Department had not determined whether Huang was acting as a Chinese intelligence agent.
China has rejected the espionage allegations, while Megaspeed has denied wrongdoing.
Meanwhile, Nvidia’s board has initiated an independent investigation into the controversy.
The disclosures arrive as Chinese AI companies seek additional computing capacity amid tightening American export restrictions.

passages: Companies linked to alleged Chinese spy Alice Huang have invested in Chinese artificial intelligence firm DeepSeek and committed to supplying Nvidia's Blackwell chips, according to a report by The Information.Blackwell is Nvidia's latest generation of graphics processing units (GPUs) and AI accelerators.

Built on the company's Blackwell GPU microarchitecture, it succeeds the older Hopper architecture and is designed to power large-scale artificial intelligence, heavy-duty data centres and high-performance computing.Alice, also known as Alice Wang or Huang Le, is a Chinese businesswoman whose links with Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang and Singapore-based data centre company Megaspeed have come under scrutiny.Meanwhile, Singapore authorities have issued Alice a stern warning and barred her from re-entering the country after finding that she provided inaccurate information during investigations into Megaspeed.Singapore's Ministry of Home Affairs (MHA) said the Singapore Police Force (SPF) assessed that Alice had attempted to mislead investigators to downplay her role in the company.The probe centres on suspected false declarations involving the purchase of servers and other related offences.

Bitcoin's latest decline has triggered another wave of forced position closures as traders using leverage struggle to maintain bullish bets. Institutional demand has also weakened. Bitcoin fell below $68,000 on November 13, extending its sharp November correction as leveraged liquidations approached $1.5 billion and institutional demand remained under pressure. BTC touched approximately $67,568 during early trading before recovering toward $68,000-$69,000. The move followed Thursday's breakdown below $72,000 , turning the previously important $70,000 level into a potential resistance zone. According to CoinGlass liquidation data , approximately $1.47 billion in cryptocurrency positions were liquidated over 24 hours, including around $1.31 billion in leveraged longs. The figures highlight how forced selling has amplified the broader market downturn. Bitcoin's latest decline has triggered another wave of forced position closures as traders using leverage struggle to maintain bullish bets. Approximately $798 million in crypto positions was liquidated over one four-hour period, with long positions accounting for $718.5 million. The selling follows earlier warnings about Bitcoin futures exposure , when outstanding positions exceeded $50 billion and liquidation risks increased around $72,000. Institutional demand has also weakened. According to Farside Investors , spot Bitcoin ETFs recorded $299.8 million in net outflows on November 11, followed by a preliminary $47.7 million withdrawal on November 12. Across the six trading sessions from November 5–12, reported withdrawals total approximately $1.49 billion. The latest selling extends an earlier weekly ETF exodus , which had already undermined Bitcoin's recovery prospects before the current liquidation wave. The cryptocurrency selloff has coincided with worsening sentiment across US technology stocks and growing expectations of tighter Federal Reserve policy. October's hotter-than-expected inflation report strengthened expectations of another interest-rate increase, while Treasury yields above 5% increased the appeal of dollar-denominated assets. Higher borrowing costs can reduce demand for speculative investments, adding pressure to Bitcoin during periods of falling liquidity. Meanwhile, Strategy's removal from MSCI indexes has added uncertainty around corporate Bitcoin treasury companies. The expected index-related selling concerns Strategy shares rather than mandatory sales of its underlying BTC holdings. The combination of institutional withdrawals, leveraged liquidations and macroeconomic pressure helps explain why Bitcoin has failed to sustain recent recovery attempts. Bitcoin's immediate technical outlook remains fragile following the loss of $70,000 support. The $67,500–$68,000 region is the first area to monitor. A sustained breakdown beneath the recent intraday low could expose $66,000, followed by the psychologically significant $65,000 level. passages: Bitcoin price has fallen below $70,000 for the first time since August, dropping more than 6% as a stronger US dollar, renewed technology stock selling and over $1.2 billion in crypto liquidations weighed on the market.
As previously reported by crypto.news, Bitcoin had already slipped below $73,000 on November 12 as Nvidia's leadership crisis unfolded.
According to crypto.news market data, Bitcoin (BTC) traded near $68,750 early Friday, November 13, after briefly falling to nearly $68,500 on Binance.
Bitcoin traders suffered approximately $677 million in liquidations, with long positions accounting for most losses.
Bitcoin liquidations exceed $677M The selloff triggered substantial losses in cryptocurrency futures markets, particularly among traders who had borrowed funds to bet on rising prices.
Long positions represented more than 96% of Bitcoin's liquidations, showing how heavily the decline affected traders expecting prices to recover.
The decline continues a pattern of lower highs and lower lows, with Bitcoin losing the $75,000 and $70,000 levels.
Meanwhile, the decline followed Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's resignation, continued withdrawals from US spot Bitcoin exchange-traded funds and fresh geopolitical concerns involving Iran and Bahrain.
He argued that Bitcoin's recent correction had not erased its recovery from the $60,000 lows.
Higher interest rates can make cash and interest-bearing investments more attractive relative to assets such as Bitcoin, which does not pay interest.
Investors were watching another development involving Strategy, the largest publicly traded corporate Bitcoin holder.
However, the index decision does not directly require Strategy to sell its Bitcoin holdings.
Liquidations occur when exchanges automatically close leveraged positions after losses reduce the collateral supporting them below required levels.

extraction.body: Bitcoin price has fallen below $70,000 for the first time since August, dropping more than 6% as a stronger US dollar, renewed technology stock selling and over $1.2 billion in crypto liquidations weighed on the market. Bitcoin price fell below $70,000 as the US dollar approached its highest level since 2025. Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's resignation coincided with renewed selling across technology stocks and cryptocurrency markets. Bitcoin traders suffered approximately $677 million in liquidations, with long positions accounting for most losses. US spot Bitcoin ETFs recorded $299.8 million in withdrawals on November 11, led by BlackRock. According to crypto.news market data, Bitcoin (BTC) traded near $68,750 early Friday, November 13, after briefly falling to nearly $68,500 on Binance. Ethereum slipped below $2,000, while XRP approached $1 and Solana traded below $80. Meanwhile, the decline followed Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's resignation, continued withdrawals from US spot Bitcoin exchange-traded funds and fresh geopolitical concerns involving Iran and Bahrain. Bitcoin price has lost roughly 45% from its October 2025 record of $126,198. Selling pressure intensified as investors responded to a stronger dollar and growing expectations that the Federal Reserve could raise interest rates again in December. The US Dollar Index climbed above 103 on Thursday, reaching its highest level in approximately 19 months. Treasury yields moved higher after stronger-than-expected inflation figures raised expectations of further monetary tightening. Higher interest rates can make cash and interest-bearing investments more attractive relative to assets such as Bitcoin, which does not pay interest. Technology stocks faced separate pressure after Nvidia confirmed that Jensen Huang had resigned as chief executive and board member. Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress took over as interim CEO. Nvidia shares fell following the announcement, while concerns about the company's leadership weighed on sentiment toward technology and AI-related investments. As previously reported by crypto.news, Bitcoin had already slipped below $73,000 on November 12 as Nvidia's leadership crisis unfolded. Investors were watching another development involving Strategy, the largest publicly traded corporate Bitcoin holder. The planned removal could force passive investment funds tracking those indexes to sell Strategy shares. However, the index decision does not directly require Strategy to sell its Bitcoin holdings. Bitcoin liquidations exceed $677M The selloff triggered substantial losses in cryptocurrency futures markets, particularly among traders who had borrowed funds to bet on rising prices. According to CoinGlass liquidation data, cryptocurrency exchanges liquidated approximately $1.23 billion in leveraged positions over 24 hours, affecting more than 151,000 traders. Bitcoin accounted for roughly $677.5 million, including approximately $653.5 million in long positions and $24.1 million in shorts. Long positions represented more than 96% of Bitcoin's liquidations, showing how heavily the decline affected traders expecting prices to recover. The largest reported single liquidation was a BTC-USD position worth $31.09 million on Hyperliquid. Liquidations occur when exchanges automatically close leveraged positions after losses reduce the collateral supporting them below required levels. Forced closures can add selling pressure while prices are falling, particularly when several leveraged positions reach their liquidation thresholds around the same price. Farside Investors data showed that US spot Bitcoin ETFs recorded $299.8 million in net withdrawals on November 11. BlackRock's IBIT accounted for $269.7 million of those outflows, bringing the total withdrawals across five consecutive trading sessions to approximately $1.44 billion. The Iranian military said the operation followed an alleged air attack on a telecommunications tower in Sirik, southern Iran. Iranian state media described the attack as retaliation, although US and Bahraini authorities had not immediately confirmed the reported damage. Oil prices did not immediately record a comparable surge, with West Texas Intermediate crude trading near $88 per barrel during the reported developments. Bitcoin price prediction as analyst Doctor Profit remains bullish Bitcoin's daily chart shows BTC trading near $68,750 after falling from an opening price of $71,460 to a low of $68,500. The decline continues a pattern of lower highs and lower lows, with Bitcoin losing the $75,000 and $70,000 levels. Despite the latest drop, crypto analyst Doctor Profit maintained his bullish outlook in a November 13 post on X. He argued that Bitcoin's recent correction had not erased its recovery from the $60,000 lows.
